POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:23:19 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 EU prepares for a grim future with new climate-proofing law  https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-prepare-future-new-climate-proofing-law/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:30:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9227222 BRUSSELS — Hope for the best, prepare for the worst.

The European Commission updated its approach to dealing with climate change along those lines on Tuesday with a package aimed at improving the bloc’s response to mounting disasters such as extreme heat, supercharged storms and worsening wildfires. 

Unveiling its first-ever law to boost the bloc’s resilience to global warming, the EU executive conceded that merely slashing planet-warming emissions is insufficient as climate extremes wreak havoc across the continent. 

“There is no alternative to continue to cut emissions more forcefully and to move full-frontal into clean energy,” Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told reporters. “But at the same time, we do have to acknowledge that the problems we’re facing have morphed into something that is so large that just doing that alone unfortunately no longer is good enough.” 

The Commission’s proposed Climate Resilience Law asks governments to draft plans to prepare for a world that’s 2 degrees Celsius hotter in 2050 and 3C hotter by the end of the century, aligning with the United Nations’ latest projections that current global climate policies can only limit warming to 2.8C. 

The same U.N. report also warned that the world can no longer limit warming to 1.5C, the lower bound of the Paris Agreement’s dual goals, and that steep emissions cuts are needed to achieve the best-case scenario of halting the rise in global temperatures at 1.8C. 

The Commission insisted that Tuesday’s package did not amount to Brussels resigning itself to catastrophic levels of warming. 

“Let me just be crystal-clear on the 1.5C, that remains our goal,” said Hoekstra. “At the same time, it would be unwise not to prepare for… the current trajectory the world is on.” 

Regulation for the deregulation era

Under the proposed law, governments are “encouraged” to take the 3C scenario into account when designing policies, budgets and investments. 

Countries will have to carry out national climate risk assessments every five years starting in 2029, and subsequently draw up climate-proofing plans by the end of 2030. These strategies should also indicate which public authorities are in charge of managing certain climate risks to avoid inaction and finger-pointing among ministries and agencies.  

The fairly light-touch legislation reflects the prevailing mood in the EU. Brussels itself has committed to a deregulation agenda, and national governments have called for fewer rules, not more, particularly where climate and the environment are concerned. 

Efforts to improve resilience to weather extremes, such as flood prevention or urban greening, are also largely a national and even local responsibility, with the EU holding limited powers. 

Even the limited rules proposed on Tuesday are already raising eyebrows. 

“I strongly support a clearer allocation of responsibilities,” said Peter Liese, the lead climate lawmaker of the center-right European People’s Party. But, he added, “we need to examine whether the plans, in the form proposed by the Commission, are necessary. Plans alone do not protect people and could tie up resources unnecessarily if we do not design them pragmatically.” 

Others argued the law was too limited. “The danger is a framework that tells us exactly how exposed we are and then commits us to nothing,” said Greens-affiliated lawmaker Kai Tegethoff. “Europe needs binding resilience targets and clear, measurable goals for the sectors most at risk.”

The Commission, for its part, has sought to appeal to governments’ concerns over the EU’s economic competitiveness by emphasizing the wealth-destroying threat of climate disasters and the business potential of climate-proofing technologies. 

“Some may say resilience is expensive. But the right question is, what is the real cost of being unprepared,” said Teresa Ribera, the Commission’s executive vice president in charge of the green transition. Both she and Hoekstra cited data showing the impact of heat on GDP as an example. “Europe cannot be competitive without being resilient,” she added. 

In the wider package presented Tuesday, the Commission also highlighted the emerging market for climate technologies such as drought-resilient crops and cooling solutions, casting European industry as a front-runner in that sector. 

As the EU is currently negotiating its next long-term budget, the package does not come with any funding attached, despite financing often acting as the biggest barrier to climate-proofing efforts. The bloc needs to invest around €70 billion a year by 2050 to adapt to a warmer world but currently only spends €29 billion. 

More where that came from

While presenting new obligations for governments, the Commission also promised to push ahead with work in Brussels. 

The European Environment Agency will draw up bloc-wide climate risk assessments, with the next one due in June 2028, and the Commission will present an EU “strategic plan on climate resilience” by the end of September 2028. 

Progress will be assessed regularly based on four criteria — climate-related deaths, economic losses attributable to global warming, the share of uninsured losses, and related fiscal costs. The Commission’s Eurostat agency will start compiling EU-wide statistics on climate-related deaths and economic losses by the end of 2030, according to the regulation. 

Beyond the legislative efforts, the EU executive also presented a wider package that includes several digital tools, including a “climate viewer” that converts the new warming scenario into local projections policymakers can use.

The Commission also vowed to take into account the new 3C warming scenario in all its future policy proposals. Further steps, including a heat wave action plan and a climate insurance alliance, are planned for next year, it said. 

“I wouldn’t say that we’re nearly done,” said Hoekstra. “Much of this is going to be work in progress.” And if climate change continues getting worse, he added, “this package might well need to be beefed up.” 

]]> en Frontex soll soziale Medien auf Hinweise zu illegaler Migration überwachen https://www.politico.eu/article/frontex-soll-soziale-medien-auf-hinweise-zu-illegaler-migration-ueberwachen/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:01:49 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9227231 BRÜSSEL – Die Europäische Kommission stellte am Dienstag Pläne für eine umfassende Reform von Frontex vor. Damit sollen die Befugnisse und Kapazitäten der Agentur im Kampf gegen irreguläre Migration ausgeweitet werden. Künftig soll Frontex eine größere Rolle bei der Rückführung von Menschen ohne Aufenthaltsrecht übernehmen und Rückführungsmaßnahmen auch außerhalb der EU durchführen können. Zudem soll die Behörde neue Kompetenzen bei der Überwachung sozialer Medien erhalten.

Welche Rolle soziale Netzwerke bei der Verbreitung von Informationen spielen, die irreguläre Migration begünstigen können, zeigte sich im Juli in der spanischen Exklave Ceuta. Dort hatten innerhalb weniger Stunden Tausende Migranten unerlaubt die Grenze überquert.

Nach den neuen Plänen soll Frontex ein Zentrum zur Überwachung und Reaktion auf Online-Inhalte einrichten. Dieses soll öffentlich zugängliche Beiträge in sozialen Medien auswerten, um Entwicklungen zu erkennen, die für den Schutz der EU-Außengrenzen relevant sind. Darüber hinaus soll die Stelle Maßnahmen gegen illegale Online-Inhalte unterstützen, die mit Sicherheitsrisiken an den Grenzen zusammenhängen, erklärte die zuständige EU-Kommissionsvizepräsidentin Henna Virkkunen am Dienstag vor Journalisten.

Die Behörde werde zudem „als vertrauenswürdiger Melder im Rahmen des Gesetzes über digitale Dienste fungieren, illegale Inhalte an Online-Plattformen melden und die nationalen Behörden gegebenenfalls auffordern, Anordnungen zur Entfernung dieser Inhalte zu erlassen“, erklärte die Kommission in einer Pressemitteilung.

Der Status als „Trusted Flagger“ ist im DSA vorgesehen, dem europäischen Gesetz zur Regulierung digitaler Plattformen. Er wird von den zuständigen nationalen Digitalaufsichtsbehörden vergeben. Meldungen solcher vertrauenswürdigen Hinweisgeber müssen von den Plattformbetreibern vorrangig bearbeitet werden.

Virkkunen kündigte an, dass Frontex den entsprechenden Status bei den nationalen Behörden beantragen werde. Angesichts der besonderen Fachkenntnisse der Grenzschutzagentur rechne sie mit einer Zulassung.

Such a deal would mark a concrete step toward closer ties amid broader discussions about cooperation on arctic security and the EU’s potential offer of “associate member” status to Canada. The summit will aim to highlight deepening ties between like-minded partners.

The signing follows a September visit to Ottawa by EIB President Nadia Calviño, during which she took the first steps toward establishing a permanent Canadian presence for the bank.

The imminent framework agreement is significant given that the EIB typically operates only in developing countries or members of the EU or the European Economic Area.

Earlier this year, Canada offered G7 members “priority access” to its critical raw minerals stockpile, according to a letter seen by POLITICO. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has also said he wants to boost EU-Canada cooperation on critical raw materials.

]]> en EU divisions persist on ‘associate member’ label for Canada https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-still-split-on-associate-member-label-for-canada/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 13:07:17 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9227048 BRUSSELS — The EU was split Tuesday over whether to offer “associate membership” status to Canada, with several countries refusing to sign off on a statement containing that phrase just 48 hours before a summit between the two sides in Montreal.

After EU capitals could not agree on the language in the statement in talks between ambassadors Monday, they used the so-called silence procedure on Tuesday. That meant a new text would be adopted automatically without a formal meeting or vote, if no countries objected by midday.

But Germany, which is leading the push to have the term “associate member” fully removed from the text, was among at least four countries that broke the silence procedure before that deadline, said two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. That means the topic will be discussed Wednesday at another meeting of EU ambassadors, just one day before the EU-Canada summit kicks off.

The fracture shows how divided the EU remains on the idea of “associate membership,” which European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during her State of the Union speech in Strasbourg last month.

Four EU diplomats told POLITICO at the time that she did not consult European capitals before floating the idea.

Von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa, the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas and a host of commissioners will fly to Montreal for a summit with Carney on Thursday and Friday, aiming to deepen ties and cooperation on everything from trade and energy to education and the Arctic.

]]> en Frontex gets power to track migration talk on social media https://www.politico.eu/article/frontex-track-migration-talk-social-media/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 13:07:12 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9226886 The EU’s border agency, Frontex, will be able to monitor social media for information about migration flows.

The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled a revamp of Frontex, strengthening its capabilities and capacity to tackle illegal migration. It will play a more prominent role in deporting people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory and new oversight on social media.

The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where thousands of migrants illegally crossed the border within a few hours in July.

The new rules will create within Frontex “an online monitoring and response center to monitor publicly accessible social media content to detect developments relevant to external border management, and also to support action against illegal online content linked to border security risks,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told reporters on Tuesday.

The agency will also “be acting as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act, flagging illegal content to online platforms, and requesting national authorities to issue removal orders where appropriate,” the Commission said in press material.

Being a “trusted flagger” under the DSA, the EU’s landmark social media rules, is a special status granted by national digital regulators. Content flagged by entities with this status is put on a fast track to be dealt with by online platforms.

Virkkunen said Frontex will apply for this status with national authorities, and she expected the border agency to be approved because of its “special expertise.”

]]> en French government mulled blocking social networks and mobile internet amid protests https://www.politico.eu/article/french-government-mulled-blocking-social-network-amid-protests/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 12:32:19 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9226139 PARIS — The French government explored ways of blocking social networks during last Saturday’s protests, two people familiar with the plan told POLITICO.

In the week leading up to Oct. 24, the French interior ministry was in touch with telecom operators to explore ways of cutting access to social networks or even to mobile internet in specific areas to prevent rioters from coordinating, according to one government official from the Prime Minister’s office and one employee of a telecom company.

The push culminated in Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu directly asking French telecom operators to be ready to block access to TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and X, in a letter revealed by French digital outlet Blast, which first reported on the government’s request.

Contacted by POLITICO, officials from Lecornu’s office, the technology ministry and the interior ministry did not deny the move nor the letter’s existence.

The government feared that the scenes of violence seen on Oct. 17 could repeat or escalate on the following weekend — a concern that did not materialize, as far fewer incidents were recorded on Oct. 24.

“What they wanted, above all, was to block the communication channels that allow gangs to meet up and organize,” said the employee of a telecommunications provider, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

The move, however, would have also prevented peaceful protesters from communicating as well. Blocking access to social networks in a targeted area, such as a specific neighborhood, is not technically possible, while cutting access to mobile internet would cause major disruptions to other key services such as mobile payments, security-surveillance devices and emergency communications.

The government also considered a less radical solution that would disable geolocation display features “to prevent gatherings of people who don’t know each other, for example,” according to the official from the prime minister’s office.

Other limitations on social media access are being discussed in parliament as part of the debate on the so-called “who breaks pays” bill, which would hold people who “knowingly took part” in a riot financially responsible — whether or not they committed property damage themselves.

The same bill would require platforms to remove within 24 hours content that incites physical or sexual assault, theft, destruction, or property damage, “when such content is likely to cause a serious disturbance to public order” and within one hour content that encourages insurrection.

Other lawmakers are proposing measures ranging from tracking troublemakers via algorithmic video surveillance to penalizing online marketplaces that fail to prevent the sale of stolen goods.

]]> en French MPs will vote on Sánchez-style amnesty plan for undocumented workers https://www.politico.eu/article/france-vote-amnesty-plan-undocumented-workers/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:46:57 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9226313 PARIS — Lawmakers in the French National Assembly will vote on a Socialist Party proposal to grant amnesty to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 unauthorized immigrants employed in France.

The measure is expected to be supported by center-left presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann, whose campaign is eager to find some breathing space between centrist candidates like Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, his rival on the radical left. Glucksmann has previously expressed support for such a step in multiple interviews.

The proposal, introduced by Socialist lawmaker Paul Christophle, hails Spain’s Pedro Sánchez for having “chosen to provide foreign nationals with the legal means to settle and work” instead of “trying — in vain — to control migration flows.”

Earlier this year, Spain moved to grant legal status to half a million unauthorized immigrants who could prove they had been living in Spain for at least five months, could provide proof of employment or a familial link to the country and did not have a criminal record.

Christophle wants to grant legal status to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 people who have been employed in France for over six months but without proper documentation.

The bill is likely to unite left-leaning MPs in the French National Assembly, but opposition from center-right and far-right groups means it will probably fail.

However, Glucksmann’s campaign hopes the proposal will highlight a rift between lawmakers backing French President Emmanuel Macron and voters who elected him in 2022 — some of whom are more progressive on issues like immigration.

The debate on immigration will be an effective way to differentiate Glucksmann from his center-right rival Édouard Philippe, who believes that amnesty plans should be contingent on a European agreement, said an official who is backing the center-left MEP. It might also help poach Macron voters “who are completely opposed to a closed society,” he added.

Among those who voted for Macron in 2022, 29% plan to vote for Raphaël Glucksmann next year, according to a Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO, against 49% for Édouard Philippe.

Glucksmann is currently projected to receive 13% of the overall vote, according to the poll, against 16% for Philippe. They both trail far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen (33%) and Mélenchon (18.5%). The top two candidates will advance to a runoff if no one wins a majority in the first round.

The bill is scheduled to be voted on Nov. 19.

]]> en Leaders of Finland and Norway hold direct talks with Putin https://www.politico.eu/article/leader-finland-alexander-stubb-and-norway-jonas-gahr-store-talk-to-russia-vladimir-putin/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 27 Oct 2026 09:59:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9226193 Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a joint call with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Tuesday as part of international efforts to secure an end to the war in Ukraine.

“The discussion was frank and substantive,” said Stubb in a statement after the call. “We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.”

The conversation was held in consultation with Kyiv and the two leaders — who are firm allies of Ukraine — were not speaking as official representatives of Europe as a whole.

But the call comes at a delicate moment in the four-year-long war as European officials bid for a place at the negotiating table, with U.S. President Donald Trump pushing for a peace deal. Two EU officials said the President of the European Council, António Costa, had been told of the planned call in advance.

Talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine are planned to take place in Abu Dhabi next month.

Støre said the two European leaders stressed the importance of de-escalation in the call with Putin. “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations,” he added.

Stubb’s office described the call as a follow-up to talks in Oslo on Oct. 20, in which the two European leaders were joined by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, who then traveled to meet Putin in Russia the following day.

The Kremlin issued a dry statement simply confirming that “the sides exchanged views on the resolution of the Ukrainian crisis,” and that settling the conflict was the main topic of Tuesday’s call. The statement added that the outcome of Putin’s talks with Witkoff was also taken into account, according to Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency.

Stubb and Støre are close friends and speak frequently, and they were together in Helsinki for the conversation with Putin. According to a statement from the Finnish president’s office, the two leaders wanted to tell the Russian leader directly that they would continue supporting Ukraine and that peace negotiations must resume, looking ahead to the planned meetings in Abu Dhabi.

They also told the Russian leader that they had a shared interest in the stability of the Baltic Sea region and the High North.

Stubb and Støre briefed Zelenskyy after the call. “I am grateful for the detailed briefing and for their active support for our diplomacy and the peace efforts we are pursuing together with all our partners,” the Ukrainian president said in a post on X. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure.”

“We discussed preparations for the trilateral meeting planned for November at the team level — Ukrainian, American, and Russian,” Zelenskyy said. “Finland and Norway, as countries that border Russia, have a particular interest in sound and reliable security arrangements. We also discussed various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security.”

Not everyone was impressed with Stubb and Støre’s move. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very skeptical” about the initiative. European countries had not been involved in coordinating the call, she said, adding: “I believe we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone.”

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement” of Russia, and if the talks lead to this then they will be welcome. But previous attempts to talk to Putin have not delivered progress and there are no signs he wants a truce, Kristersson added.

Paula Pinho, spokesperson for the European Commission, said: “We take note of the call, which took place solely on a bilateral basis, and is a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo.” The EU side is “united in our commitment not only to put an end to this horrific war but to achieve peace that will be just and sustainable,” she said.

“That is our aim and that is the stance we are defending in the ongoing talks. These negotiations are happening in different formats, different places and different levels involving heads of states and government, ministers, senior diplomats and officials. The EU is involved.”

The last staunch European supporter of Ukraine to speak to Putin at leader level is believed to have been French President Emmanuel Macron in July 2025. Some EU leaders like Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico and former Hungarian premier Viktor Orban have maintained semi-regular contact with the Russian president in recent years, despite the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

EU diplomats and officials have been considering how to ensure Ukraine’s allies in Europe can play a meaningful part in negotiations on a ceasefire and longer term peace agreement. Stubb’s name emerged as one of the potential leaders who could take on the job of representing Europe and bolstering Ukraine in face-to-face talks with Trump and Putin.

He is one of the few EU leaders and Ukraine backers who has maintained a healthy relationship with Trump at a time of strained relations across the Atlantic. Finland also shares a 1,300 kilometer border with Russia, meaning Stubb and his officials already have valuable experience of dealing with a threatening and unpredictable neighbor.

Sebastian Starcevic contributed reporting. This article has been updated.

Reynolds told POLITICO at Labour conference that a return to the bloc’s customs union — one of the potential EU options floated by Burnham since then — would force “a whole range of alignment on regulatory issues” and warned that constant “constitutional questions” cause “a lot of uncertainty for business.”

But, challenged by Sky News Tuesday on whether Burnham was adding to that uncertainty by bringing the Europe issue to the top of the government agenda, Reynolds said: “I don’t disagree with the prime minister …

“For the here and now, I very strongly backed our manifesto position which is: can we improve our trade relationships with the rest of the world, which we’ve done.”

He added: “When we’re talking about the next ten years, you can’t avoid this question.
The uncertainty is there come what may. I want as least uncertainty as possible for British business.”

Burnham is due to attend a long-planned U.K.-EU summit in Brussels on November 20, where he will attempt to iron on issues with the existing Brexit settlement — although the summit is not expected to get into wider questions about the U.K.’s relationship with the bloc.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:38:07 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 [Interview] There are still more American soldiers than Western ones on Nato’s eastern border, says defence expert Robert Pszczel https://euobserver.com/244667/interview-there-are-still-more-american-soldiers-than-western-ones-on-natos-eastern-border-says-defence-expert-robert-pszczel/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:16:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244667 Donald Trump’s 9 October diesel deal with Vladimir Putin left Europeans - including Ukraine - out in the cold, as US dollars will now become key aid in the financing of Russia's war.]]> Donald Trump’s 9 October diesel deal with Vladimir Putin left Europeans – including Ukraine – out in the cold, as US dollars will now become key aid in the financing of Russia’s war. 

In the meantime, hybrid attacks using drones and sabotage are escalating across Europe. Intelligence agencies warn Russia will be escalating them in the next months, and even consider a “limited military attack”, as Danish intelligence warned late September.

EUobserver spoke to Robert Pszczel, former Nato information bureau chief in Moscow, about European defence and information strategy.

Pszczel is a long-time Polish diplomat in Warsaw and Brussels, now working with a Polish think tank, Centre for Eastern Studies (Ośrodek Studiów Wschodnich, OSW).

He closely follows Russia’s hybrid war and European defence strategy.

We see the US deprioritising Europe in their defence and diplomacy. What should our response be?

Let’s not mix our views of this administration’s policy with our strategic relations with the US. Why would we want to help with the process of decoupling? Do we want to give people in the US administration who marginalise the value of alliances arguments for disengagement?  Because for me, that’s what ramblings about a European Defence Union do. The paradox is that this idea really appeals to die-hard MAGA isolationists because it gives them an excuse for undermining the Nato alliance.

]]> Europe is in denial about war — and that’s how wars start https://euobserver.com/245150/europe-is-in-denial-about-war-and-thats-how-wars-start/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:30:59 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245150 Europeans have not experienced war for so long that they don’t recognize it anymore, and don’t see it coming. That was also the case just before the outbreak of the First World War.]]> This year, in France, a small book was published with major implications for the future of Europe: Notre déni de guerre [Our Denial of War] written by a military historian, Stéphane Audoin-Rouzeau.

Audoin-Rouzeau specialises in a subject that was long regarded a niche field: the First World War.

He delves into facts, developments, and societal, political and social undercurrents that are long past and therefore seem of little concern to most people.

But according to him, these matters are more relevant to modern Europeans than ever before. The more time passes, the more parallels he sees between the period around the First World War and the times we now live in.

With one very significant parallel: the denial that war is drawing nearer.

His argument is that Europeans have enjoyed peace for so long that they no longer know what war is. They don’t recognise it, cannot see it coming and therefore don’t know how to avert it.

Many have come to believe that if they don’t attack anyone or declare war on anyone, no one will attack them in return – the typical logic of people who have only known peacetime.

Europe’s problem, in his view, is that not everyone in the world lives in peacetime, and that others therefore operate according to a different logic – the logic of wartime.

]]> Partial victory for disabled rights, as some carers may board flights for free from 2027 https://euobserver.com/245083/partial-victory-for-disabled-rights-as-some-carers-may-board-flights-for-free-from-2027/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:02:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245083 Under newly-agreed rules expected to come into force in 2027, airlines will decide whether or not companions to disabled passengers are deemed necessary for safety reasons. Only if their presence is required will their ticket be free, while companions traveling with disabled passengers anyway will have to pay for a full-price fare.]]> New EU legislation will waive airfares for people accompanying disabled passengers if the companion’s presence is deemed required by the airline.

Updated passenger rights greenlit by MEPs last week (20 October) close a loophole allowing airlines to turn away passengers with reduced mobility.

Once approved, agreed changes mean airlines will allow disabled people the opportunity to travel with companions free of charge – if required for safety reasons – from 23 October 2027.

Ministers in the council had proposed alternative legislation that would allow airlines to collect taxes and charges for required companions. But in a win for disabled rights, negotiators for the European Parliament succeeded in insisting such charges be waived.

Rapporteur Matteo Ricci, an Italian MEP for the Socialists & Democrats (S&D), called the decision a “significant step forward” following the vote in Strasbourg.

This comes after a previous vote in July required airlines to fully cover the replacement of mishandled mobility equipment and allow people with disabilities or reduced mobility to sit next to their companions at no extra charge.

Read more

Free cabin bags and stronger protections: What the EU’s air passenger deal means for travellers

Companions not required by airlines must pay

Under new rules, passengers already travelling with an accompanying person not required by airlines – such as a personal assistant to help with their needs – will still need to pay for an extra ticket.

This was not made clear by Ricci who told reporters last week: “All people with disabilities or reduced mobility will have the right to have a companion traveling with them free of charge.”

In reality, the text adopted at plenary allows airlines to determine based on safety judgements whether or not companions of disabled people can travel for free.

So under new rules, many people with disabilities may not be able to bring companions free of charge.

“This leaves a gap for passengers who need personal assistance, but whose accompaniment is not required by the airline,” said Maltese S&D-group MEP Alex Agius Saliba. The co-chair of parliament’s disability group told EUobserver: “Their support needs are no less real, and the additional ticket can remain a financial barrier.”

Advocacy group the European Disability Forum (EDF) said when a provisional agreement was reached that updated enforcement of passenger rights offers “insufficient protection” for disabled passengers.

Disability rights whack-a-mole 

Daniel Casas, policy officer at the EDF, thinks new rules are a step in the right direction.

]]> Farming ministers agree on more national control of EU funds as part of CAP reforms https://euobserver.com/245084/farming-ministers-agree-on-more-national-control-of-eu-funds-as-part-of-cap-reforms/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:02:21 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245084 The bulk of EU agriculture subsidies are set to distributed via a new system of national and regional plans, as governments seize control of the bloc's subsidy scheme.]]> Ministers want to speed up and simplify the payment of farming subsidies by taking control of the EU’s multi-billion euro farming payment schemes, under a deal reached late on Monday night (26 October).  

The agreement at a meeting of EU agriculture ministers in Brussels finalises the negotiating position of EU governments on the future of the bloc’s Common Agricultural Policy in its next seven-year budget. 

The ‘negotiating box’ prepared by the Irish EU council presidency earlier this month for the 2028-34 multi-annual financial framework spared agricultural subsidies provided by the common agricultural policy from cuts worth a total of €141bn but proposed three-percent cuts, worth €24.6bn, to funding for National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP), which are intended to streamline the distribution of EU cash to governments for a variety of different policies including agriculture and fisheries. 

Read more

MEPs warn Irish EU budget plan is ‘short‑sighted’ and risks ‘historic failure’ as cuts of €141bn spare farm and cohesion funds

The idea behind the NRPPs is to set up one single fund to provide support for farmers.

Each EU country would be expected to develop a single comprehensive plan outlining the reforms and investments it intends to implement from 2028 to 2034 and how it plans to use EU funds. 

EU governments agreed on Monday that this planning process should be designed to give them far greater autonomy. They say that the recommendations the commission makes to member states regarding the design of support programs should not be binding.  

The new system is set to prioritise ‘active farmers’, which sets a threshold of a minimum level of agricultural activity for farmers, as well as young farmers and small farmers.

]]> Listen: What should we expect from the Israeli elections? https://euobserver.com/245094/listen-what-should-we-expect-from-the-israeli-elections/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 09:28:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245094 Israelis are heading to the polls today for legislative elections. It is the first national vote since 2022, and a decisive moment for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is running again.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

Israelis are heading to the polls today for legislative elections. It is the first national vote since 2022, and a decisive moment for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is running again.

So who are the main candidates, and what is actually at stake? First, a quick look at where we are.

A lot has happened since the last elections in 2022. Since the Hamas terrorist attack on 7 October 2023, which killed more than 1,100 people, the Israeli government has cracked down on Gaza: the death toll is at 74,500 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. The number of people wounded is triple that.

While a ceasefire was signed last year, around 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since then. In the West Bank, settlement expansion has accelerated, with growing violence. Over the past three years, more than 10,000 Palestinians have been displaced.

Read more

I led Israel’s oldest peace group and advised the Knesset. Netanyahu may fall on Tuesday, but the West Bank annexation policies won’t

So this is the context in which the elections are taking place. The current prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is running for re-election, as there is no term limit for prime ministers in Israel. And he is no newcomer: he has spent around 16 years in power, though not consecutively.

Now, what do the polls say? According to several surveys published last Friday, Gadi Eisenkot is slightly ahead of Netanyahu. But neither is expected to reach an absolute majority.

So who is Gadi Eisenkot? He is Netanyahu’s rival, but politically he is closer to the current government’s line than you might expect.

He is a former chief of staff of the army, and he also served in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for several months after the 7 October attack.

He later left, accusing the prime minister of mismanaging events, and in particular of failing to anticipate the attack.

His son was killed in the war in Gaza in December 2023, which seems to have given him a certain sympathy among the public.

Read more

Israel’s election may disappoint everyone, as Brussels and Washington face a hard reckoning with a more ‘centrist’ leader

On the Palestinian question, he opposes the creation of a Palestinian state, and he does not challenge Israel’s policy of territorial expansion. He only promises to tackle settler violence, in the name of the rule of law.

Then there is the duo Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. Bennett briefly served as Prime Minister in 2021. The duo represent a centre-right line that does not differ hugely from Netanyahu’s.

On the left side of the political spectrum, there seems to be only one candidate: Yair Golan, of the Democrats party. He is the only one calling for the recognition of a Palestinian state.

He is also the candidate many Israelis abroad are coming home to vote for. The French daily newspaper Le Monde has published a long article interviewing Israeli expatriates around the world.

Most of them back Golan, who, according to several of those interviewed, represents the only hope of putting Israel back on the right track. But the polls suggest he is well behind the right-wing candidates. He would win around 10 seats in parliament, against 22 for Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for Likud, Netanyahu’s party.

Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up https://euobserver.com/245049/one-supply-scare-pushed-china-into-renewables-two-real-crises-still-havent-woken-europe-up/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245049 The mere threat of losing control of one maritime strait turned China into a clean tech powerhouse, while Europe, hit by two real energy shocks in a few years, is wasting time watering down its green rules.]]> In 2003, Chinese president Hu Jintao worried about what became known among the country’s leadership as the ‘Malacca dilemma.’  

Some 80 percent of China’s imported crude passed through the Malacca strait which Beijing’s naval forces could not control. 

This gave rise to a wider security doctrine of supply-chain resilience which became the basis for China’s transformation into the clean tech powerhouse it is today. 

When the US–Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern oil flows this year, Xi Jinping called China’s early bet on wind and solar “forward-looking” – as recounted in a new paper from the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute published on Monday (26 October). 

The paper identifies green growth as “the answer” to geopolitical uncertainty. Clean tech isn’t just clean, it’s also secure and not dependent on imports. Plus, it delivers a “more durable pathway” to “economic resilience.” 

Some governments want to expand fossil-fuel imports, or drill more oil or gas wells, arguing that a more diversified supply chain improves resilience. But the paper dismissed that. 

Oil and gas are priced on global markets, so even producers are exposed to price shocks. More North Sea drilling would save UK households between £16 and £82 (€19 to €98) a year, the paper finds, citing Oxford University research, compared with £105 to £441 on a renewables and electrification pathway.

It’s interesting comparing how the two political systems respond to (hypothetical) supply shocks. In China, the mere threat of losing control of one strait was enough to transform energy politics gradually over many years.

]]> One-in-three European voters now support an authoritarian or populist party, new research reveals https://euobserver.com/245034/one-in-three-european-voters-now-support-an-authoritarian-or-populist-party-new-research-reveals/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:21:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245034 A historically-high number of voters have chosen parties classified as authoritarian or populist, according to a new report analysing parliamentary election results for 260 parties in 31 countries since 1946, or since the year free elections were first held.]]> A historically-high number of voters have chosen parties classified as authoritarian or populist, according to new research looking at 31 countries across Europe, not just the EU.

Germany saw the starkest rise, with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) getting over 20 percent of the last national parliamentary vote, while in contrast parties classified as radical left split the 13.8 percent of votes between them.

The Authoritarian Populism Index, published by two European think tanks, EPICenter and the Nordics-based Timbro late last week (22 October), analyses parliamentary election results for 260 parties in 31 countries since 1946, or since the year free elections were first held.

The high support for populists is a result of mainstream parties not being able to “adequately address the concerns of our time,” Emelie Franzén, EPICenter’s research coordinator, told EUobserver.

The populists’ success is a “result of a lack of trust towards the elites,” Mateusz Michnik, economic analyst for EPICenter, told EUobserver. He also added that populists are more effective communicators than mainstream parties, especially in crisis situations, such as the Covid pandemic, the migration wave of 2015, or Russia’s 2022 attack on Ukraine.

Read more

Listen: How close is the AfD to governing in Saxony-Anhalt?

The Index has been classifying populist parties since 2016, defining them as groups where representing the people above the elite is “a central organising principle of their political worldview,” the author says.

Reinhard Heinish, political science professor in Salzburg, told EUobserver that the report “combines different hard-to-measure concepts, and needs to interpreted with some caution.”

Despite this overarching characteristic, their profile is far from uniform, the report’s author, Andreas Johansson Heinö, Timbro’s director, warned.

“Most are culturally conservative, while economically they are almost evenly divided between left and right.” The populist parties included in the study tend to be eurosceptic, but only a minority supports leaving the EU, he added.

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, about 10 percent of Europeans chose authoritarian or populist leaders. Since 2000, the number started to increase, reaching just under 30 percent in 2019.

Now, parties outside of the political mainstream have seats in 11 out of 31 European governments.

“Populists can ‘infect’ other political parties with populism,” Michnik said, which he thinks explains a surge of anti-migration policies across the continent.

Contrary to Germany, Bulgaria, and Norway, which recorded the largest increases in the past years, Hungary’s score radically decreased with the April elections that brought an end to Viktor Orbán’s rule.

Though his adversary has failed to acknowledge defeat, EU leaders and pro-democracy groups expressed relief at the unexpected comeback.]]> In a historic turn of electoral tides, Brazil’s incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated far-right opponent Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday (25 October,) alleviating fears that a Bolsonaro-dynasty comeback would topple the world’s fourth-largest democracy. 

Following a disastrous first-round election for Lula on 4 October, in which he narrowly lost a majority in Brazil’s national congress, the Workers’ party leader overturned predictions to become the first president to win the second round of voting after losing the first one.

First-round voting gave 47 percent for former president Jair Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio, and his rightwing Liberal Party, whose voters mainly represent wealthy and emerging middle classes in the south of Brazil, as well as evangelical Christians, one of the largest religious groups in the country. 

Lula’s northeastern, working class, multi-racial support base only made up 45 percent of all primary votes, but climted to 51.8 percent in Sunday’s second-round of the presidential election. 

Despite setting a record in being the first Brazilian president to win four non-consecutive terms, Lula’s triumph still leaves room for possible conflict. 

Bolsonaro, whose campaign capitalised on continuing the work of his divisive father, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, refused to concede defeat – leaving an open window for history to repeat itself. 

Read more

Trump cheers Bolsonaro Jr’s advance on Lula in Brazil, but EU fears for Mercosur alliance

“We’ll request the annulment of these elections,” Bolsonaro told the press after votes had been counted, accusing Brazil’s Supreme Court of having “changed the rules of the game in the middle of the game,” by ordering polls to stay open for two more hours on Sunday.

What Brazil’s nationalist candidate declared as “unacceptable” was an idea initially intended to facilitate all Brazilians’ attendance at the polls, since multiple areas were reported to have been affected by public transport problems. 

Bolsonaro’s issue with the courts is another link in the chain of power-hungry promises he had made during his campaign to “re-democratise this country”.

Without guidance on what that could mean beyond his publicised desire to extend the duration of presidential terms, many voters fearfully associated his remarks with a potential coup, or with Jair Bolsonaro’s infamous liking for authoritarian rulers – including Brazil’s own 1964-1985 dictatorship.

]]> Ex-EU commissioner Reynders faces new Belgian and Polish scrutiny after EUobserver revelations https://euobserver.com/244962/ex-eu-commissioner-reynders-faces-new-belgian-and-polish-scrutiny-after-euobserver-revelations/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:59:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244962 EUobserver revealed last week that a director in the Belgian intelligence service had exchanged WhatsApp messages with ex-EU commissioner Didier Reynders, which may have been part of a criminal conspiracy to block reports into Reynders' alleged wrongdoing.]]> Some Belgian spies have questioned EUobserver’s report of a cover-up in favour of an allegedly corrupt Belgian ex-EU commissioner, while international commentary focused on his possible Russia ties.

EUobserver revealed on Friday (23 October) that Hugues Brulin, a director in the Belgian intelligence service (VSSE), had exchanged WhatsApp messages with ex-EU commissioner Didier Reynders, which may have been part of a criminal conspiracy to block VSSE reports into Reynders’ alleged wrongdoing.

But according to “several” VSSE sources who spoke to Belgian daily Le Soir, Brulin, who had been the number three in the VSSE hierarchy, had been in charge of logistics, Human Resources, and IT, but did “not have the power to block enquiries or put his nose into dossiers”.

Brulin did have access to secret dossiers only in case the number one and two directors in the VSSE were absent, and he had to sign off on special operations, called “BIMs” in VSSE jargon, which included measures such as phone wiretaps or home intrusions to place bugs, but this situation occurred just once during his tenure, Le Soir said.

But even if that was all true, Brulin still used to have the power to end the careers of VSSE officers who had looked into Reynders, on grounds of flimsy infractions, as happened in at least three cases, according to EUobserver’s sources.

Read more

[EXCLUSIVE] Leaked WhatsApps between ex-EU commissioner Reynders and senior Belgian spy reveal attempts to bury allegations of his possible Russia ties

“This article feels like a liberation. I don’t know if it really is one, but it feels like one … Thanks again in the name of all the normal, honest, taxpaying Belgians,” one ex-VSSE contact told EUobserver, commenting on last Friday’s revelations.

And besides which, there are allegations that Reynders had other VSSE insiders who might have been better placed to act.

    ]]>         Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll https://euobserver.com/244879/serbias-student-protestors-win-parliamentary-majority-setting-scene-for-showdown-with-vucic-for-decembers-presidential-poll/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:25:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244879 Serbia’s student movement has broken Aleksandar Vučić’s decade-long hold on parliament.]]> “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future,” said Radomir Sajčić, professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters on Sunday’s evening (25 October). “The voice of the people is being heard”.

    The student-backed list won Serbia’s parliamentary election at the weekend, in a vote that amounts to the biggest challenge so far to president Aleksandar Vučić’s long-standing grip on power.

    And that night, Vučić (unexpectedly) acknowledged defeat. “Vox populi, vox dei,” [The voice of the people is the voice of God], he said, marking a significant moment in the Serbian political landscape that Vučić has dominated for more than a decade.

    The 56-year-old politician served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017, then won the 2017 and 2022 presidential elections. Critics accuse him of authoritarianism, control over the media, and manoeuvring between the European Union, Russia, and China.

    However, this years historic turnout (nearly 70 percent ), the highest since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1992, has overturned his SNS party (Serbian Progressive Party).

    In the 250-seat parliament, the Student’s List will have the majority – 140 seats, and second comes Vučić’s SNS with 104 seats. The remaining seats will be shared mainly between ethnic national-⁠minority parties.  

    “It was effectively a referendum on president Aleksandar Vučić,” the Serbian pro-democracy group Kreni-Promeni, who backed the Students’ List, told EUobserver.

    From student protests to electoral change

    The opposition was unable to seriously challenge Vučić in the previous parliamentary elections, partly because of its fragmentation. However, a significant turning point in Serbian politics came in November 2024, when 16 people died after a canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad.

    Read more

    Serbian students and diaspora maintain pressure for Vučić to call elections, with no EU help

    The tragedy then sparked massive demonstrations across Serbia, led primarily by students. Hundreds of thousands of people took part. They blamed the disaster largely on the government and its corruption.

    The student protests gave rise to Vučić’s main challenger in this year’s elections: the Student List (SL). The 250 candidates running for parliament included individuals selected by students, primarily academics.

    “The students have selected prominent citizens – experts in their own fields,” Miloje Savić, a volunteering poll observer, told EUobserver. “They know which values they are supposed to protect and represent,” he added.

    The student electoral list was led by Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.

    The weekend result thus represent a major political breakthrough for a movement that emerged less than two years ago from protests against the government’s long-standing corruption.

    For the SNS, this defeat is “a huge blow to him [Vučić]”, senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, Jelena Vasiljević told EUobserver.

    But, as the poll winner and Vučić’s most successful opponent, the SL is not out of the woods yet.

    Students smeared as ‘blockaders‘

    Even as he acknowledged defeat, Vučić continued to use the same online rhetoric, referring to winners as the “students’ blockade list”. Vučić also warned of investor uncertainty and damage these results might have on the gas trade.

    Taken together – the language and the economic warnings – offer an insight into how the SNS and Vučić will depict the incoming government.

Having worked as a parliamentary adviser in the Knesset and later as executive director of Peace Now, I know how that can happen.

    Many of the parties seeking to replace Benjamin Netanyahu are avoiding clear positions on the Israeli-Palestinian question, but some of their candidates may end up overseeing annexation they never campaigned for.

    Israel’s previous coalition, led by Naftali Bennett in 2021, offers a warning.

    Called the “government of change” because it ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run in office, it brought together a variety of parties, from Bennett’s rightwing party to Labor and Meretz, leftwing parties.

    Its answer to profound ideological disagreements, particularly over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, was to preserve the status quo. The coalition lasted roughly 18 months, and although it changed the tone of government, it left much of the policy towards the West Bank intact.

    Read more

    No candidate in Israeli election backs a Palestinian state. The EU’s answer is more ‘reforms’, not pressure

    For example, Merav Michaeli, then Labor leader and transport minister, opposed settlement expansion.

    Yet her ministry continued to implement previously approved infrastructure commitments, including substantial budgets for roads facilitating that expansion.

    Through my work at Peace Now, I saw how the coalition’s status-quo agreement constrained her ability to challenge projects inherited from the previous government. A minister could thus find herself implementing a vision she opposed.

    Today, the stakes are higher.

    Another slice of the West Bank

    Consider E1, between Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, where construction would threaten Palestinian territorial contiguity and the viability of a future Palestinian state.

    The government has advanced tenders for all 3,401 planned housing units, with crucial stages of the tender process set to be completed before a new government takes office.

    E1 exemplifies wider efforts to establish difficult-to-reverse facts: new settlement outposts, including in areas under Palestinian civil administration, expanding settlements and administrative changes that entrench Israeli control.

    A successor government would have to intervene actively to reverse them.

    These developments are backed by an explicit political vision. The current government’s guidelines and coalition agreements assert exclusive Jewish rights throughout the land of Israel and commit to advancing Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank.

    Under Bezalel Smotrich, serving as a minister within the defence ministry, a new settlement administration and civilian positions have been established, shifting significant aspects of West Bank governance from military administration to civilian political control.

    These structures will not disappear when their architects leave office. The far-right has equipped the state with both a vision and the machinery to advance it.

    Inertia is not neutral when the machinery is already moving in one direction.

    Parties seeking to replace Netanyahu need not necessarily agree on a final-status agreement with the Palestinians, but they must find enough common ground to commit to halting annexation and reversing the structures that enable it.

    Those understandings belong in coalition negotiations, when parties still have leverage, rather than in battles left for individual ministers once they are in office.

    Nor is this a distant constitutional question. Palestinians in the West Bank already face systematic violations of their basic rights and freedoms, from restrictions on movement and access to land to violence and forced displacement. Each new settlement and outpost deepens this injustice and makes the prospect of a political settlement more remote.

    Facts on ground

    The entrenchment of permanent Israeli control is creating a reality that is increasingly difficult to reverse, making political intervention more urgent with every passing year.

    The current government’s response to growing international pressure illustrates the danger.

    After the UK announced measures targeting settlements, foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar ordered the closure of its consulate in East Jerusalem. Britain considered expelling Israeli diplomats in response, and a compromise left a much smaller British mission operating.

    The episode illustrates Netanyahu’s vision of a ‘Super Sparta’: an Israel preparing itself for international isolation rather than addressing the policies contributing to it.

    A future government seeking to change that trajectory should start with two tasks.

    ‘Messianic minority’

    First, it must take seriously the reasons behind international sanctions and address the policies driving them, including settlement expansion and settler violence. A messianic minority must not be allowed to drag Israel into international isolation and economic decline.

    Second, the government should help European partners distinguish between Israel and the settlements, including through transparent supply chains and clear proof of origin, so that restrictions aimed at settlements do not spill over into the broader Israeli economy.

    Both tasks require urgent and concrete policy changes, beyond a more moderate diplomatic tone.

    European governments should not expect a new coalition, or even international sanctions themselves, to bring about these changes automatically. They need to make their expectations explicit, press prospective coalition partners to incorporate concrete commitments into their agreements, and judge the resulting government by its actions.

    Read more

    Israel’s election may disappoint everyone, as Brussels and Washington face a hard reckoning with a more ‘centrist’ leader

    Without that pressure, politicians who never endorsed annexation may become useful idiots for a project they do not support, helping to consolidate a single undemocratic state in which millions of Palestinians are permanently denied equal rights and freedoms.

    Preventing that outcome requires urgent political action, while a different future is still possible. Neither Israelis seeking change nor their European partners can afford to assume it will happen on its own.

    In both Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD won the elections a few weeks ago. But it does not have an absolute majority in either regional parliament.

    As for the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AFD has no prospect of forming alliances to secure a majority, and negotiations are well under way between the Social Democrats, the Greens and the Left Party to reach an agreement. Together, they hold an absolute majority.

    But the situation is quite different in Saxony-Anhalt. What will most likely happen, is an alliance with the BSW, the party founded by Sahra Wagenknecht.

    The BSW describes itself as radical left, fighting for social justice. But in practice, it takes a very hard line on migration. And it is also notably lenient towards Russia.

    Read more

    AfD’s electoral triumph is a watershed, regardless of whether it gets to form the Saxony-Anhalt government

    In the end, the BSW and the AFD share similar views on a number of things, so they have been talking to build a coalition. They haven’t announced any deal whatsoever for now.

    But there are two things we should look at. First, the election of the AfD candidate as president of the regional parliament in Saxony-Anhalt.
    Tobias Rausch is the first AfD member to be landtag president.

    He won thanks to votes from the AfD and the BSW. This would have been enough. But he even got 4 more votes.

    Together, BSW and AFD have 44 votes, while Rausch received 48. That means at least four votes came from other parties, which are not supposed to cooperate with the far right. Some suspect they came from the CDU. But as Friedrich Merz pointed out, the ballot is secret, so there is no way to verify that.

    Now, president of the regional parliament is not a particularly powerful position. But still, it is the first time the AfD has won it, and it came as a shock in Germany earlier this month.

    So does this mean the same thing will happen when the regional prime minister is chosen? Well, not necessarily. The vote could take place in December. No date has been set yet. So there is plenty of time to negotiate a deal.

    Read more

    Can the EU survive with far-right leaders running major member states? The answer is worrying

    But the fact that the AfD and the BSW managed to agree on the parliament’s president shows that an agreement is conceivable.

    There is something else worth noting. The two parties have just voted together on a non binding resolution on the war in Ukraine. In it, they call on Ukraine to capitulate to Russia, and demand an end to financial support for Kyiv.
    So again, this shows they share several positions.

    And in the end, even if the AfD doesn’t manage to get its candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, elected as head of the state, the AfD and the BSW could still form a majority on many votes, just as they did on the resolution about Ukraine.
    Which would mean a change of policy for the region.

    Before we wrap up, you might be wondering: what powers do German states actually have? Quite a lot, in fact. Education and culture, police and public security, media as well, since regional public broadcasters, for example, are governed by the states.

    Each state has its own government. And the regional prime minister leads it, much like a prime minister would, at national level. The states are also represented in the Bundesrat, a kind of senate, which takes part in drafting national laws.

    So yes, and AFD led regional government would mean a shift in local policies.

]]> Huit startups, deux lauréates

Huit startups franciliennes étaient en lice lors de cette étape. Comme à chaque étape du Fundtruck, les entrepreneurs disposaient de trois minutes pour présenter leur projet, avant cinq minutes de questions face à un jury composé de 14 membres issus notamment de l’investissement, de l’entrepreneuriat et de l’accompagnement des startups.

À l’issue des délibérations, les pépites Femnov et Up&Charge se sont qualifiées pour la Grande Finale après une double égalité, une deuxième fois cette saison. Femnov, cofondée et dirigée par Marilyn Rolfe, développe un dispositif médical logiciel destiné à assister les praticiens dans l’analyse des échographies endovaginales afin de détecter des pathologies gynécologiques, dont l’endométriose. Up&Charge, cofondée et dirigée par Marin Champenois conçoit elle des bornes de recharge par induction, sans câble, pour les véhicules électriques.

Une nouvelle étape francilienne

L’événement a pu compter sur le soutien de la BRED Banque Populaire, ainsi que de Bpifrance, IVECO, Electra, CF Advisory et CF - Compagnie Fiduciaire, avec Manuel Biota, et sur l’accueil de la CCI Seine-Saint-Denis.

Femnov et Up&Charge rejoignent désormais les autres lauréats de la saison et se préparent à défendre leurs chances lors de la Grande Finale du Fundtruck 2026, qui se tiendra le 26 novembre prochain. La tournée, elle, se poursuit avec une nouvelle étape à Bruxelles.

      <title>Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-stock-market-filing-takeaways</link>
      <description><p>The AI company’s first public financial disclosures reveal explosive growth, huge costs and risks ranging from cyber-attacks to the limits of safeguards</p><p>Anthropic <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-files-listing-stock-market">has filed</a> to go public on the US stock market, revealing for the first time the AI research lab’s financials and all the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively affect its business.</p><p>The company’s investor prospectus, released on Monday, veers from hyperbolic predictions about AI’s “incredible potential” to existential risks of the technology to the reality of its current business: explosive but incredibly expensive growth. The filing to US financial regulators, known as an S-1, provides the public’s first look at an audited version of Anthropic’s finances.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-stock-market-filing-takeaways">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom</p><p>Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.</p><p>The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June.       <title>The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z</link>
      <description><p>People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans</p><p>Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.</p><p>Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 27 Oct 2026 15:53:30 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Irish retailers that fail to display prices for paper bags risk legal action, says watchdog]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/retailers-failing-to-display-prices-for-paper-bags-face-legal-action-ccpc/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/retailers-failing-to-display-prices-for-paper-bags-face-legal-action-ccpc/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 12:24:33 +0000Irish retailers are failing to display the prices they charge for paper bags and similar products and risk legal action unless they address the issue, the consumer watchdog has warned.

The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has written to retailers around the State, reminding them of their legal obligations when it comes to price transparency.

It warned that they could face fines and court appearances unless they display clearly what costs consumers are likely to face for all elements of their purchase.

In 2002, a tax was attached to plastic bags which currently stands at 22 cent.

There was some reluctance in the early days, but the tax was quickly embraced and after its introduction there was a dramatic reduction in the number of discarded plastic bags across the State.

In the year before the levy was rolled out, plastic bags made up as much as 5 per cent of the litter in Ireland, compared with less than 0.3 per cent now. The levy was revenue neutral with all the money raised going back into environmental measures.

Supermarkets subsequently phased out the so-called single-use plastic bags and have been charging more than 70 cent for heavier-duty plastic bags. The advantage for these is that bags that cost over 70 cent incur no levy, which means the shops make money on every single bag they sell.

Since 2023, many retailers – including Brown Thomas, Arnotts, Marks & Spencer, Zara, H&M and Eason – have all started charging for paper bags, with most claiming they are doing so out of concern for the environment.

The CCPC said that consumers have been contacting its helplines “indicating that there is no display signage in store or around the checkout area showing the price of shopping bags for sale”.

Under consumer law, retailers must clearly display prices for items being sold. These prices must be unambiguous, easily identifiable, clearly legible and on or near the product.

The CCPC said that where “breaches of the law are detected, [it] may take further action to ensure retailers comply with price display laws and consumers are properly informed when shopping. These actions range from the issuing of fixed payment notices and compliance notices up to prosecution in the courts.

“Retailers must comply with consumer law, and consumers have a right to know the price of any product they purchase, including shopping bags,” said the watchdog’s director of communications and consumer information, Aoibhín de Búrca.

“They should not be put on the spot at the till to pay it or notice it afterwards on their receipts.”

She said the contacts the CCPC had received “through our helpline highlight potentially concerning practices around price displays, so we are writing to traders to remind them of their legal obligations”.

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[PureGym seeks planning on two Dublin sites as it eyes entry to Irish market ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/puregym-seeks-planning-on-two-dublin-sites-as-it-eyes-entry-to-irish-market/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/puregym-seeks-planning-on-two-dublin-sites-as-it-eyes-entry-to-irish-market/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:43:10 +0000PureGym is considering two locations in Dublin city centre as the springboard for the British group’s expected entry into the Irish market in the new year.

The private-equity-backed gym chain made its first attempt to enter the Irish market more than 10 years ago, although it ultimately never broke ground on approved plans for two north Dublin sites.

The gym operator has now lodged planning applications with Dublin City Council to establish two outlets, both of which would operate as 24-hour facilities for the chain of “no-frills” fitness centres.

One gym would occupy a part-ground floor and basement unit in the Parnell Centre shopping complex in Dublin 1, about 500m from O’Connell Street, a recently filed planning application shows.

Mainly occupying the basement, the plans comprise a main gym floor, changing rooms, an additional exercise and training area, and a free weights zone, according to a letter from the council’s planning and development department assessing the application.

Planners have sought additional information from the company before deciding on the application.

The other proposed outlet is located in the College Square commercial development, fronting on to Tara Street in Dublin 2. At 82m high, College Square is the tallest habitable building in the State. The council is yet to hand down a decision.

PureGym works out on IPO to fund global expansion

A spokesperson from PureGym said the company plans are “still in the early stages, and both sites are subject to planning approval. However, we have ambitions to open both gyms in the first half of 2027.

“These gyms will expand access to low-cost, high-quality fitness in Dublin, while also creating a number of employment opportunities,” the spokesperson continued. “We know there is strong demand for gym memberships that are both affordable and flexible.”

Planning records dating back to 2016 show PureGym sought planning permission to establish an “24-hour, 7-day a week gymnasium” with “new illuminated signage” in Smithfield Market in Dublin 7.

Following objections from local residents and businesses, that case was referred to An Bord Pleanála (now An Coimisiún Pleanála), the State’s planning authority.

It ultimately granted the company permission for the development, but not the signage.

At the time, the company said the State was “likely to be well-suited to the PureGym customer proposition and operating model” of low-cost membership fees and stripped-back facilities.

It is understood PureGym reconsidered an entry into the Irish market after Britain voted to leave the European Union later in 2016.

Founded in 2008, PureGym now operates 728 gyms worldwide, according to its website, about two-thirds of which are located in Britain. It also operates in Denmark, the United States and Switzerland, and has franchised outlets in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

It closed a deal in early October to acquire a Swiss gym chain for £233 million (€279 million).

]]><![CDATA[H&M overcomes online sales dip to report 13% rise in pretax profit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/hm-overcomes-online-sales-dip-to-report-13-rise-in-pretax-profit/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/hm-overcomes-online-sales-dip-to-report-13-rise-in-pretax-profit/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:39:38 +0000Online sales dipped at the Irish arm of clothing retail giant H&M last year but that failed to dent profits which jumped by 13 per cent to €4.36 million.
