]]>olaser<![CDATA[Wholesale electricity prices surged 93% in a year ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/27/wholesale-electricity-prices-surged-93-in-a-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/27/wholesale-electricity-prices-surged-93-in-a-year/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:18:29 +0000Wholesale electricity prices almost doubled in the past year, new data from the Central Statistics Office showed, as the war between US and Iran pushed energy costs higher.

But prices remain below the peak recorded in the wake of Russia’s war against Ukraine, falling by 53 per cent from August 2022.

On a monthly basis, wholesale electricity prices rose almost 7 per cent in September, with energy fuels up almost 11 per cent compared with August.

The cost of energy fuels has risen almost 47.6 per cent year on year compared with September 2025.

Domestic producer prices have also risen, with costs for manufactured goods rising by an average of 2.4 per cent last month compared with September 2025, while producer prices for exported goods rose 8.1 per cent. Manufacturing producer prices in general were 7.4 per cent higher year on year.

Food product prices were up 1.2 per cent over the year, with the wider food products, beverages and tobacco index rising 1.1 per cent. Among the biggest changes were in the fish and fish products sector, where prices rose 9.6 per cent, while meat and meat products fell by 9.4 per cent.

Wholesale prices for chemical products saw a 16.5 per cent increase in prices, while electrical equipment prices were up 6.1 per cent. Construction product prices rose 0.9 per cent rose by 3.8 per cent in the 12 months since September 2025.

“Wholesale price inflation showed an increase in September 2026 with a 0.5 per cent growth in the overall producer price index for manufacturing industries in the month,” said Deirdre Toher, statistician in the prices division.

“The price index for export sales was up by 0.5 per cent since August 2026, while the index for home sales was unchanged in the month.”

]]>Gareth Fuller<![CDATA[Small PTSB shareholders ‘paying for Minister’s exit’ in €1.6bn takeover deal, court hears]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/minister-driven-by-commitment-to-exit-banking-sector-when-voting-to-sell-ptsb-court-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/minister-driven-by-commitment-to-exit-banking-sector-when-voting-to-sell-ptsb-court-told/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:30:45 +0000Minister for Finance Simon Harris was “driven by the State’s commitment to exit the investment”, not by the desire to achieve the best possible price for shareholders, when he voted in favour of the proposed sale of PTSB to Austrian banking group Bawag in July, the High Court has heard.

There was “an issue of special interest” when the Tánaiste and Fine Gael leader supported the €1.6 billion offer, a PTSB minority shareholder, Piotr Skoczylas, told Justice Michael Quinn.

He is one of four shareholders objecting to the proposed acquisition at a High Court sanctioning hearing today.

Quoting the Coalition’s commitment in the programme for Government of “normalising”, or leaving, the Irish domestic banking market, Skoczylas said, “this is not a State secret, it’s known to all its citizens”.

“I don’t blame the Government for wanting to exit this investment, because they are not bankers – they are the Irish State. The Irish State is not in the position to manage Irish banks”.

Skoczylas is the managing director of Scotchstone Capital, which owns a stake in PTSB of less than one per cent. He is opposing the proposed deal to sell the bank – Ireland’s third largest domestic bank in which the State currently holds a 57.5 per cent stake – to Bawag.

“I am paying, as a tiny shareholder, for the Minister’s exit – he should be paying for his own exit,” Skoczylas said, later pointing to a “turnout of 30 per cent” at the emergency general meeting in July to vote on the bid.

With the State’s majority share, it was “simply engineering a situation where other shareholders do not matter – despite the fact that they are objecting to the scheme”, he said.

Lyndon MacCann SC, the barrister acting for the Minister for Finance, responded to Skoczylas’ oral submission by saying: “It’s easy to make an assertion, it’s different to supply evidence”.

“That’s all very interesting, but it has no value” to the case at hand, he said.

“There is no evidence that the Government policy resulted in the State accepting a price that it ought to not have accepted,” he said, and it is “not a matter of controversy that the State has had a policy for some time to exit the banking sector.”

The court heard earlier in proceedings that Axis Capital, the corporate advisory firm cofounded by former banker Mark Duffy, would not seek an adjournment of legal proceedings to delay the sale.

The company had indicated last week it would do so in order to allow time for a “large global investment manager” it had been introduced to by an investment bank to conduct “its confirmatory due diligence” before it submits a rival bid to buy the bank.

“It is my understanding this morning they are not pursuing that, but would like the court to consider what they have to say,” said Kelley Smith SC, the barrister acting on behalf of PTSB.

Duffy, a former chief executive of Bank of Scotland Ireland, appeared in the courtroom alongside Lutz Hartmann, a Frankfurt-based international lawyer representing Axis Capital.

“We have followed directors and have submitted correspondence to you,” Hartmann said to Judge Quinn. “It is not our intention [to act] in any way from what the rules permit.”

“While we do not request [an adjournment] any more, we do wish to present facts,” to the court, he said.

]]><![CDATA[Dublin Airport operator selects LDA boss John Coleman as new chief executive]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/daa-selects-lda-boss-john-coleman-as-new-chief-executive/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/daa-selects-lda-boss-john-coleman-as-new-chief-executive/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:19:19 +0000DAA, the State-owned operator of Dublin and Cork airports, has appointed Land Development Agency (LDA) chief executive John Coleman as its new chief executive, replacing Kenny Jacobs, who stepped down earlier this year.

Coleman will be in situ for seven years, DAA said in a statement on Tuesday, and will take up the role early in 2027.

He joins from the LDA, the Government agency established to strategically manage and develop housing on publicly owned lands, since its establishment in 2018. Coleman also previously served as chief financial officer at the National Asset Management Agency (Nama).

DAA chairman Gary Owens said Coleman is being appointed “following a comprehensive selection process”.

“His familiarity with navigating complex planning and regulatory systems will also be of great value to DAA as we progress our plans for the long-term development of Dublin and Cork airports,” Owens said.

Coleman said he was “honoured and excited” to join the airport operator. “Throughout my career, I have been driven by a belief that strong infrastructure, strong institutions and strong stakeholder partnerships are essential to national progress.”

In a separate written statement put out by the LDA, Coleman said his role at the agency was “a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to establish an organisation focused solely on tackling one of the biggest challenges facing our country”.

He said the LDA had “made great progress” in its first eight years.

The LDA said the process to find Coleman’s successor will “commence in the coming weeks”.

Details of Coleman’s contract and pay have not yet been disclosed. However, based on previously reported figures, he is in line for a roughly 13.6 per cent increase in his basic salary once he takes up the position.

Earlier this year, the executive renewed his contract with the LDA and received a €50,000 increase in his basic salary, bringing it to €250,000. Jacobs, meanwhile, received a basic salary of €284,235 at DAA in 2025. He also received pension contributions and other taxable benefits of €90,595.

Coleman joins DAA after Jacobs stood down from the top role earlier this year, amid disagreements with the State-owned airport operator’s board.

Jacobs, a former Ryanair executive, sued DAA in the High Court in January after he was suspended by the company in December 2025, pending an investigation into allegations made against him.

He settled the action in February, agreeing to “voluntarily step down” from the position.

This followed Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien’s refusal to sign off on an exit package, known to amount to a figure of close to €1 million, for Jacobs that had emerged from mediation between both sides.

In a separate statement on Tuesday, the minister said Coleman is taking on the role at DAA at “an important and challenging time for DAA”.

“I worked with John during the previous Government, when he led the LDA, advancing the delivery of affordable homes and maximising the use of State-owned land,” former housing minister O’Brien said. “His leadership made an important contribution to addressing Ireland’s housing needs, and I want to acknowledge and thank him for his work and achievements at the LDA.”

]]>Nick Bradshaw / The Irish Times<![CDATA[How Irish businesses operating in both the North and South face ‘unnecessary’ barriers]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/businesses-that-export-cross-border-are-more-profitable-more-resilient/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/businesses-that-export-cross-border-are-more-profitable-more-resilient/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000Crá, the successful Irish language TV detective series telling the story of a garda and a podcaster’s investigation into the discovery of a body in a bog in Donegal, tells us much about changing patterns in cross-Border trade.

Made by Fíbín Films, the TG4 and BBC Northern Ireland co-production begins its second series on November 3rd following the success of the first series – one that has so far been sold into 68 markets internationally.

“Though backed by TG4, we were short about 30 per cent of the budget to make it and we just simply couldn’t have made it without going north of the Border. Drama is a very expensive business,” says Bernie Hoban of Fíbín.

With the help of BBCNI and Northern Ireland Screen, the funding gap was closed, though the rules stipulated that the Northern contribution had to be spent north of the Border.

Post-production for the first series was carried out by the Belfast-based company Zoogon, but on the back of the successes to date Fíbín has now set up its own operation in Belfast.

“There are no barriers in our industry to people we can hire. For example, if we need a grip guy, we can hire him from Belfast, or if we need a writer, we can hire them from Myanmar, or wherever,” Hoban tells The Irish Times.

However, other companies are not so fortunate. “When I speak to other industries, there seem to be a lot of barriers,” Hoban says. “If they want to hire an electrician from Northern Ireland, they can’t because qualifications aren’t recognised south of the Border.

“If the two jurisdictions came together to recognise that a plumber is a plumber, an electrician is an electrician, that all qualifications are recognised, it would open up the island.”

In Castleblayney, Co Monaghan, the difficulties about cross-Border qualifications recognition are seen daily by Ohk Energy’s Una McCabe, the electrical company’s training and development manager.

Offering example after example , McCabe tells of one employee who recently qualified as a qualified certifier (QC), signing off on electrical works that are up to standard.

The employee did his apprenticeship in Northern Ireland, but his QC training took place in the Republic. “We are now trying to get him certified in the North as a QC, and his qualification isn’t transferring over,” McCabe says.

“They don’t speak to each other, and they are now expecting this gentleman, who has a list of qualifications, already a qualified QC, to do the course again in the North.”

Up to now, Ohk Energy has largely worked in the Republic, but recently won a significant contract with Power NI, Northern Ireland’s largest electricity provider, serving 450,000 homes and businesses.

“Businesses operating across Ireland and Northern Ireland should be able to invest in their people with confidence that those skills can travel with them. Ultimately, skills mobility is economic mobility,” McCabe says.

“If we want indigenous companies to grow, compete and create high-quality jobs across the island, removing unnecessary barriers to the recognition and development of our skilled workforce has to be part of that conversation.”

AI firm Anthropic begins countdown to IPO with prospectus filing

The problems caused by the non-recognition of qualifications are attracting increasing attention following a study of the cross-Border services trade by Oxford Economics for InterTrade Ireland.

The regulatory issues were focused on in recent weeks by officials from both sides of the Border when they were briefed on the details of the InterTrade report.

“They were immediately interested, asking for a list of the problems. It was an immediate red flag. So, anything we can do to get that message out that there’s a problem is useful,” says InterTrade’s Stuart Mathieson.

For InterTrade, however, which has promoted cross-Border trade since it was created in 1999 in the wake of the Belfast Agreement, the sharp growth in services trade is a little-known success story.

“The really interesting thing about services is that it’s growing despite us not paying all that much attention to it. If we’d paid the same amount of attention as we do to goods, it could be twice what it is now,” says Mathieson.

Official figures tell only part of the success, with Northern Ireland’s Statistical Research Agency (NISRA) reporting that services trade quadrupled from €1 billion in 2011 to €4.2 billion in 2024.

‘The focus is finding people from Ireland’: The EU’s big ask for new English translators

The growth in services – covering everything from construction to the film industry – is “outpacing” the growth in goods trade, “even as post-Brexit regulatory changes have introduced new complexity”, the NISRA says.

However, the numbers fail to capture the true scale of cross-Border services trade, since the numbers collected exclude financial services and tourism, and lag behind by a year.

Once adjustments are made, total trade in 2024 came to €6.25 billion, with Northern Ireland dominating the exchanges, with services exports to the Republic rising to €4.3 billion, while those from the Republic reached €2 billion.

And it is a story of success not well understood, most of all in Northern Ireland, says Mathieson. “Northern Ireland has a significant services trade surplus with Ireland, a massive one.

“If it had to reorient, for whatever reason, towards Great Britain, or maybe the United States, depending on whether it’s tech and things like that, the consequences would be devastating.”

What my most embarrassing job interview taught me

The Republic, says InterTrade, is “already NI’s largest non-GB export market, accounting for around 44 per cent of NI’s services exports to destinations outside the UK, a share that has risen consistently over the decade”.

“From NI’s perspective, the all-island services relationship is central to its external economic performance,” the report carried out by Oxford Economics for the Newry, Co Armagh-headquartered cross-Border says.

In all, NI’s services exports to the Republic account for just under a fifth of all services exports, placing it above most comparable “contiguous-border pairs in Europe”, as the report describes it.

The “asymmetry” in the numbers is reflected in the trade balance: Northern Ireland runs “a substantial and persistent services trade surplus” with the Republic of approximately £2 billion [€2.4 billion] a year.

Confirming the anecdotal stories of Northern Irish builders heading south in numbers every morning, the trade is skewed, with construction accounting for 55 per cent of NI’s services exports – growing by 21 per cent a year since 2011.

Highlighting the gaps in the statistics, the Oxford study finds that financial and insurance services emerge as the second-largest category in NI’s exports south of the Border, worth €750 million, approximately.

The number is partly explained by Northern Ireland’s success in the increasingly important area of cybersecurity in recent years, where firms such as Rapid7 and Proofpoint have bedded into Belfast successfully.

“We’ve got very, very good ICT companies here,” says Mathieson, as he looks out the window on to the Lagan from the Waterfront Hall in Belfast. “We’ve got a little bit of a specialism in things like blockchain, cybersecurity.”

From the Republic’s perspective, the cross-Border services trade is far less significant, amounting to less than 1 per cent of such exports, but that number is skewed by the dominance enjoyed by foreign-owned tech companies south of the Border.

However, there are signals that things are changing here, too – or that “an inflection point” has been reached, as the report puts it – because services exports from the Republic to NI increased 88 per cent in 2024.

The jump is explained by increases – to just over €1 billion – in manufacturing-linked services, construction and professional services, though whether that is “a durable structural shift, or a one-year spike” remains to be seen.

The possibilities for locally-owned firms in the Republic to begin their own “export journey” north of the Border are a key part of the Irish Government’s strategy, including co-operating with like-minded SMEs in Northern Ireland.

Our research consistently tells us the barriers are practical

Margaret Hearty

The growth in services trade over the last decade has been steep, but it is just the foundation, says InterTrade Ireland’s chief executive, Margaret Hearty: “Businesses that export cross-Border are more profitable, more resilient.

“Even more importantly, 75 per cent of them will then go on to export off the island. So, what holds businesses back? Our research consistently tells us the barriers are practical; they’re not fundamental.”

However, the barriers that are there – some left by the United Kingdom’s departure from the European Union – now see two regulatory regimes operating differently within miles of each other.

Left unattended, such divergences could get worse, since so-called active regulatory divergence has already happened in financial services and digital services, the report cautions.

In addition, there is a danger that passive divergence over years, where rules accumulate in one jurisdiction, but not in the other, will slowly bring gaps where there were none before, it goes on.

Broadly, however, the majority of firms operating on both sides of the Border find managing services contracts is “manageable and broadly straightforward, particularly where they are delivered remotely”, Hearty says.

The main barriers centre on VAT and payroll, especially for remote-working staff – an increasing headache and one that has led some firms to stop making cross-Border hires unless workers are going to be physically in the office each day, industry sources say.

In addition, Northern firms complain that there are difficulties infinding out about public procurement contracts in the Republic, despite the existence of the eTenders website.

The Belfast-based software company, SustainIQ, has successfully sold into the Republic for years, though Limerick-born co-founder Maria Diffley points to the differences that exist between Ireland and the UK for public contracts.

Unlike Ireland, the UK system has pre-qualification checks that companies can pass to be put on a list of companies that are told about the contracts coming up in their sector, “unlike eTenders, which has to be constantly watched”.

However, the difficulties are vastly outweighed by the positives, she says. “Customers appreciate that we are not remote, that we are but a drive away, and that we’ll travel if there is an issue.”

For Lisa Heavey of Dublin-based HB Label Print, which makes self-adhesive labels for the food industry and other uses, the help offered by InterTrade has been invaluable: “We got a contract from our first meeting,” she says.

Working north of the Border has been enlightening, she says. “Dublin has become quite metropolitan. Ulster people tend to be a bit anti-corporate; they like their sarcasm, their humour, and they’re straight. I appreciate that.”

]]>Kelvin Boyes<![CDATA[Renters and younger people hit harder by inflation, new CSO data shows]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/renters-and-younger-people-hit-harder-by-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/renters-and-younger-people-hit-harder-by-inflation/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 12:28:34 +0000Households led by younger people and those who are renting their homes are experiencing higher levels of inflation, new research indicates.

Central Statistics Office (CSO) figures show households headed by a person aged under 35 experienced an inflation rate of 4.4 per cent in September, “the highest of all the categories examined”.

The headline rate for the country as a whole in September was 4.1 per cent.

Households renting were also found to be experiencing a higher rate of inflation, estimated at 4.3 per cent compared with a rate of 4.1 per cent for households paying a mortgage, while it was 3.7 per cent for households that owned their home outright.

The disparity in how households experience inflation stems from the fact that lower-income households spend a higher proportion of their income on energy and rent.

“Each household has its own unique consumption pattern of goods and services and therefore its own personal experience of inflation,” the CSO’s Edel Flannery said.

The main drivers of inflation in the 12 months to September for lower income households were electricity, gas and other fuels, followed by rent and transport costs, the agency said

For higher earners, it was transport and restaurants and accommodation services costs, which includes hotels, bar sales, and takeaway food and coffees.

The CSO’s analysis showed that for the lowest 25 per cent of households by income, electricity, gas and other fuels, including home heating oil, was the largest contributor to their estimated inflation rate at 1.1 per cent of 4.2 per cent, followed by rent and transport at 0.8 percentage points each.

For top-earning households, restaurants and accommodation services and transport were the largest contributors to their estimated inflation (both 0.8 percentage points of 4.1 per cent).

The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in the last four months, but it is expected to hold fire when it meets later this week, keeping rates unchanged.

]]><![CDATA[A 97-year-old woman faces €455,000 payment to Bank of Ireland over life loan taken out in 2003]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/life-loan-proves-a-millstone-for-97-year-old-pensioner/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/life-loan-proves-a-millstone-for-97-year-old-pensioner/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000I would like to draw your attention to a very serious issue involving a Bank of Ireland life loan to an elderly lady. I am hoping that by having this case highlighted it will help speed up our efforts to have the issue resolved, and also serve as a cautionary tale to anyone else considering taking on a life loan.

Back in 2003, when she was 72, a single woman with no children received correspondence from Bank of Ireland offering her a life loan. Having taken legal advice (she never discussed this advice with anyone), she took out a life loan of €130,000.

She actually only needed €30,000 at the time, so she put €100,000 back on deposit with Bank of Ireland, where it has remained ever since. (It is not clear why she took out €130,000 when she only needed €30,000.)

As of June this year, the total amount required to close the account was a staggering €455,081. The woman is now 97.

Her nieces and nephews have been trying unsuccessfully to get mediation on this loan with Bank of Ireland since 2022. A complaint was made in August last year to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO), but in a response in May this year, the ombudsman said it could be another 12-14 months before we hear from them on this complaint.

The general public needs to be more aware of the risks involved in life loans. While Bank of Ireland no longer offer such a product, there are ads for similar products from Spry Finance frequently aired on radio.

The behaviour of Bank of Ireland at all stages of this loan needs to be questioned and answers given.

The fact that the FSPO can tell a 97-year-old that it will be 12 to 14 months before a member of the investigative team will be appointed to this case is shocking.

JC

They offered people who might be wealthy on paper due to the value of their home but cash poor – especially women with little or no pension cover – access to money that would not need to be repaid in their lifetime.

Lifeline or life sentence? How equity-release lifetime loans work

Interest built up over time and the loan was redeemed when you died or otherwise moved out of or sold the property. That interest could, and in some cases did, swallow up all the equity in a home. However, where the debt was greater than the eventual sale price, the bank committed not to chase the estate for any payment over and above the sale price.

The collapse of property prices saw them swiftly withdrawn from the market, alongside tracker loans, as banks faced the prospect of losing money on both products.

Life loans were available only to those over the age of 65. People could borrow up to 20 per cent of the value of their homes if they were in their 60s to as much as 30 per cent for those in their 80s. For someone like your friend, borrowing at 72, the limit was 25 per cent.

“To ensure customers would understand the product, the information provided clearly explained the terms of the loan,” a spokesman for Bank of Ireland says. “Most importantly,” the bank continues, “before any life loan was agreed it was a requirement for each customer to obtain independent legal advice – and to show that they had taken that legal advice – to ensure that customers fully understood the terms and conditions.”

Whatever about Bank of Ireland mis-selling this loan, there are questions about the advice any legal practitioner gave this woman back in 2003. She clearly did not “need” this money – or most of it anyway – as €100,000 has sat untouched on deposit ever since, effectively losing value. It is just such a bad call on so many levels.

So what “advice” the solicitor provided, I have no idea. I can see them saying they advised only on the legal and contractual issues rather than the wisdom of taking the loan but that seems a very narrow and unhelpful interpretation of their role.

Reader’s attempts to foil fraudsters hit weird Bank of Ireland roadblock

The bank certainly appears to be sticking to its view that the loan has worked exactly as it should and as it was advised to the client. Whether that passes muster with the ombudsman remains to be seen, especially given she borrowed money under this expensive product that she clearly did not need. How was that assessed?

Asking a 97-year-old to hold on for up to 14 months to hear if they have a case certainly seems insensitive but the resources of the ombudsman are limited and all the cases that get to the investigation stage have people who are feeling hard done by, so how can they prioritise other than first come, first served.

It is simply unfortunate that it took so long for the details of this loan to emerge so that her extended family could help her.

Indeed, an increase in the parent to child threshold means that a family with three children can now pass on an extra €60,000 tax free, or one with four children and 10 grandchildren could pass on an extra €120,000 tax free, thus saving the tax that would have otherwise arisen if the children had exceeded their thresholds.

So, what else might you need to know about changes to the inheritance, or capital acquisitions tax (CAT) regime?

Receipts on the rise

There is no doubt that the amount of CAT being collected by the Exchequer is on the rise, with the total yield surpassing €1 billion last year for the first time. This is more than double what was collected back in 2020. And inheritance tax is one of the main drivers of this, with some €968.4 million collected in 2025, up from €430.6 million in 2020, according to Revenue statistics.

More people are paying it, too. Figures show that 15,200 people paid the charge in 2025, up from 14,006 in 2024; 13,055 in 2023; and 11,376 in 2020. That’s a 25 per cent increase since 2020.

However, while there may be continued calls to increase the parent-to-child threshold further, the figures show that the biggest contributors to inheritance tax are those who leave money to relatives other than their children. The threshold for an aunt leaving money to a nephew or niece is quite low, at just €44,000. This means that a lot of the tax collected comes from this cohort – and it is on the rise.

As the table shows, so-called group B inheritances now account for 46 per cent of all receipts, compared with 41 per cent for parent-to-child transactions.

Did the changes go far enough?

The increase in the parent-to-child threshold of €20,000, or 5 per cent, will mean that someone inheriting €420,000 today, as opposed to before the budget, will save €6,600 in taxes. Group B, for transfers between relatives, also increased, from €40,000 to €44,000.

“It hasn’t really done enough in terms of where property prices are now,” he says, noting the continued increase in house prices. Today, for example, the median national price is €400,000 – or as much as €685,000 in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown.

As Donnelly puts it, a child inheriting a three-bedroom house in Dublin, with a few thousand in savings, is going to “to end up a good bit over the threshold”, which will mean facing a tax bill.

He would like to see the parent-to-child exemption moved closer to €500,000 (this level was in fact last exceeded in 2009, when the threshold rose to €542,544), or for the introduction of some sort of exemption on the family home.

Biggest benefit

Those who stand to benefit the most from the latest changes are families who can avail of either CAT business relief or agricultural relief. This is because once certain conditions are met, these reliefs reduce the taxable value of the asset for gifts or inheritances by 90 per cent.

As Donnelly notes, if you have a parent passing on shares in a company or land that’s eligible for relief and is worth €4.2 million, its taxable relief will drop to €420,000 thanks to the relief.

“The €20,000 increase in the threshold actually allows for €200,000 worth of value to transfer tax free,” he says. “That’s kind of where the main benefit is. It can be quite useful”.

Home or savings

For typical families, however, the changes don’t amount to a lot.

“It’s better than nothing but it’s not a huge amount, and it’s not going to be life changing for families,” says Donnelly.

Alison McHugh, partner and head of private client tax services at EY, agrees that the increases were “relatively modest and are unlikely to fundamentally alter estate or succession planning strategies”.

However, she adds that they are nevertheless “a welcome development”, adding that they will at least help to mitigate the impact of asset price inflation, particularly in relation to family homes and business assets.

“For a family with four children and 10 grandchildren, this will allow an additional €120,000 of value to fall outside of the charge to Irish CAT,” she says.

“[The budget] hasn’t done anything for childless asset owners. A €4,000 increase is nothing in the grand scheme of things,” says Donnelly. Indeed, the increase means that someone would save €1,320 in tax thanks to the higher threshold.

“For example, if you have no children but wish to split your estate between 10 nieces and nephews, this will allow you to give an additional €4,000 to each one, or €40,000 of value overall.”

An aspect of the recent budget that may have surprised was the decision to reduce capital gains tax to 31 per cent but to leave CAT at 33 per cent.

As Donnelly notes, if parents transfer a home to a child today, a CGT bill might arise on this transfer, while the child might face CAT, depending on their thresholds and the value of the property. This CGT can be used to offset the CAT charge but now they are being charged at different rates.

One area in which many would have liked to see change is the small gifts exemption. This has stayed at the €3,000 level for quite some time, and no change was made in the budget. “It’s a useful way for people to pass on bits of wealth,” he says.

Less often compared is how the two countries’ political systems manage their relationship with public service broadcasting. That is even less flattering, and the same excuses do not apply.

The UK has far more rigorous and transparent structures for deciding what its national broadcaster is for and how to pay for it. Chief among them is the royal charter, renewed every decade after intense scrutiny and debate at Westminster. Ireland’s approach is ramshackle, as this month’s shambolic budget handling of RTÉ’s funding demonstrated.

In Dublin, we had the Future of Media Commission, whose recommendation on funding was rejected. Whether that recommendation was wise is debatable, but it hardly justifies the procrastination that has followed.

In the UK, these questions are argued over in parliament, on a timetable fixed by the charter. In Ireland, they are settled, or not, in irate correspondence between departments, while a toothless Oireachtas committee goes in search of soundbites. Neither country faces an easy decision but, despite all its problems, the BBC is starting from a much better place.

One reason is that the UK licence fee rises with inflation under the current funding settlement and now stands at £180 (€212). The Irish fee, frozen at €160 for 18 years, would be about €195 had it kept pace with prices.

Last year, RTÉ received €183.5 million from the licence fee and €41.3 million directly from the exchequer. Indexation would have brought in roughly €40 million more, almost exactly the size of that top-up. Most of the so-called bailout was simply the cost of political reluctance to grasp that political nettle.

Only about four in 10 Irish households now buys a licence. Strip out those with no television, and the half a million or so with State-funded free licences, and somewhere between a quarter and two-fifths of those legally obliged to pay do not.

A household charge at the current rate, levied on everyone not entitled to a free licence, would raise roughly €90 million to €115 million a year more than the existing system, allowing for a reduction in the current €160 price. Richard Bruton in 2019 promised such a charge to arrive by 2024. It never did.

UK culture secretary Lisa Nandy and her Irish counterpart Patrick O’Donovan face essentially the same problems. But O’Donovan’s are far worse and that, for all RTÉ’s faults, owes less to the broadcaster than to the short-termism and procrastination of successive Irish governments.

A universal media charge would be politically unpopular and is regarded by some as regressive. It is far from clear that the organisations themselves have the capacity to remain relevant in the post-broadcast age.

TV licence fee ‘extremely difficult’ to collect if evaders not prosecuted, says RTÉ boss Kevin Bakhurst

Bermingham added that the fuels would be a critical resource for airlines and shipping and transport companies seeking to cut their dependence on fossil fuels.

“While we remain the market leader in our sector in Ireland, our business continues to evolve and diversify, with international markets making an increasingly important contribution to our overall growth.

“Our focus remains on building on this progress, delivering complex, high-value engineering projects and continuing to expand our presence across Ireland, UK, Europe and the Middle East.”

McCabe said he was “encouraged by the strength of our pipeline, with work extending into 2027 and beyond, and remain confident in the opportunities ahead”.

The global data centre boom is being driven by soaring demand for artificial intelligence (AI). Investment in AI infrastructure will hit a record $31.6 trillion through to 2050, according to baseline projections in PwC’s recent global data centre outlook report.

]]><![CDATA[French stocks: ‘Buy when there’s blood in the streets’?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/26/french-stocks-buy-when-theres-blood-in-the-streets/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/26/french-stocks-buy-when-theres-blood-in-the-streets/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:52:00 +0000“Buy when there is blood in the streets” is one of the oldest maxims of investing. France, where riots have sent shopkeepers counting the cost of looting and investors worrying about spiking bond yields, is currently putting it to an unfortunately literal test.

Right now, there’s no shortage of investors willing to wait for the blood to dry. Bank of America’s latest monthly fund manager survey shows a record number plan to underweight French stocks over the next year.

Barclays says French shares are now some investors’ biggest short position, as they bet on further declines.

French shares have lagged for years. Global equity indices have roughly doubled since the bull market began in October 2022, notes investment strategist Ed Yardeni, but the MSCI France index has risen just 36 per cent.

Down 5 per cent in 2026, France’s CAC 40 is on course for its biggest annual underperformance against the broader European market since 2010, having lagged for three consecutive years.

Political risk is not the only driver – luxury stocks like LVMH and Hermès account for a significant chunk of the index, and they have struggled amid weaker demand for high-end products – but it is an important one.

Goldman Sachs estimates around half of France’s underperformance against other European indices in recent years is explained by political risk.

Given that only around 16 per cent of CAC 40 revenues are generated in France, the sell-off might tempt contrarians. Yardeni notes the French index’s price-earnings ratio has fallen from 16 in February to 13, even as corporate earnings have hit record highs.

Analysts have raised their 2026 earnings growth forecast to 24 per cent.

European stocks extend slide as French unrest rattles investors

“French earnings have decoupled from the French economy”, says Yardeni. French banks “warrant a discount; the multinationals don’t”.

Of course, cheap stocks can also get cheaper. With the 2027 presidential election looming and France’s fiscal problems unresolved, cautious investors may prefer to ignore the advice to buy when there is blood in the streets and heed another market adage instead: don’t try to catch a falling knife.

]]>KIRAN RIDLEY<![CDATA[Across-the-board pay rise will do little to help fill key public sector posts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:38:00 +0000

Until the early 1970s, the Civil Service was a very traditional organisation that had changed little over time. There was limited movement between departments, and almost none between the public sector and the private sector.

Most people joined straight after school, there were few graduates, although many ambitious civil servants, like TK Whitaker, studied for a degree at night. Unless they were women who married [and who were effectively fired as a result], civil servants were likely to stay until they retired. Men progressed slowly through the ranks, based on seniority.

My first boss in the Department of Finance told me that when he joined it in the 1950s, he had calculated, based on the seniority rule and his colleagues’ ages, that he would spend most of his career as an assistant principal before, in the final three years before retirement, being promoted in rapid succession as a principal officer and then assistant secretary. In the event, he served as secretary general of the department for seven years.

Joining the EU meant quite a number of Irish civil servants left to work for the European Commission. The marriage bar ended in July 1973. Gradually, other reforms led to much more fluid movement across the public service.

The wider public service included graduate roles such as secondary teachers, doctors and local-authority engineers. While less than a third of public servants held third-level qualifications in 1970, those who did constituted more than half of the Irish graduate workforce.

All of this made public sector employment rather different from that in the private sector, with limited parallels in terms of pay. To a large extent, public and private sector employers were not competing to attract the same workers.

The advent of mass third level education in Ireland changed things. Few now enter the public sector straight from school. Primary teachers and nurses now have graduate qualifications. Today, three quarters of public sector workers have a third level qualification, but only constitute a third of graduate workers.

There is also greater choice, and substantial movement, between jobs in the public and private sectors. The security of a public sector job does not have the same allure when there is full employment. So the State as an employer needs to compete to attract and retain talent. That means the public sector must pay competitive rates, or some of the most able and ambitious teachers, civil servants, nurses or physiotherapists will seek better pay elsewhere.

Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says

In the run-up to the 2008 economic crash, average pay in the public sector had reached 50 per cent more than in the private sector – an excessive gap.

Following the collapse in the public finances, all public sector workers experienced painful cuts in pay. Over the subsequent decade, public service pay rose more slowly than the private sector. However, over the past few years the relationship has stabilised.

Public service workers are paid, on average, about 30 per cent more than the private sector, but this largely reflects their higher average qualifications.

The Government now needs to deliver a pay increase for public service workers, not because prices are higher but because most other workers are seeing their pay rise. Failure to keep pace with the private sector would see skilled employees leave.

The Department of Finance forecast that average pay across the economy will rise by around 4 per cent this year and next. The budget arithmetic provided for a 3 per cent public pay rise next year, so any higher pay deal will need additional funding.

The expected rise in private sector pay sets a guideline for any public sector pay agreement. If public sector workers are offered significantly more, that could push up taxes, and have knock-on effects on other pay. But if offered significantly less than their private sector counterparts, there could be an exodus of skilled staff for better pay elsewhere.

A public pay deal will be done – and here’s what it will look like

While this sounds fairly straightforward, things are, of course, more complex. Private sector pay deals are generally contingent on increased productivity. That, too, should be the case in the public sector.

Across-the-board pay increases in the public sector won’t address what’s needed to attract workers to some key areas where posts have been hard to fill – in the Naval Service, in special care, in some IT roles.

While a private employer would simply pay more, public pay agreements cannot easily handle such differentiation, but need to find a way to do so. The alternative of filling key roles by outsourcing to consultants is not an ideal one.

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[With EU presidency, Ireland has chance to implement digital identity wallet by end of year ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:27:00 +0000The priorities for Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU have been wide in scope across various sections of society, different sectors within the economy, along with competing national or common interests.

Some of those will resolve in due course under the current term, while many will either stall or progress as it passes onto Lithuania and then Greece through 2027.

One long-standing objective and policy priority that falls directly during our watch is the provision for an EU Digital Identity Wallet for all citizens and businesses by December of this year.

This is part of the wider Digital Decade Policy Programme (DDPP), which is the EU’s framework for achieving digital transformation by the end of the decade.

It includes targets in relation to digital skills, digital infrastructure, the digitalisation of businesses, and access to digital public services.

That last (but not least) area essentially involves all key public services being available online with citizens’ digital identity and ability to access services working seamlessly throughout the EU.

The practical applications are complex but the “only once” principle applies throughout, where citizens should not be repeatedly asked by governments or multiple agencies for information already available.

With progress being made on all fronts to various degrees, this is now a defining period for Ireland to help push the digital public services agenda forward for citizens, businesses and State services. Interoperable data should flow freely enough to support everything from mortgage approvals to healthcare records and planning applications.

The main challenge is one that often falls on European or cross-border projects. It comes down to collective co-ordination and consensus. Twenty-seven member states, with as many starting points, governance structures, all building toward the same targets along separate paths that sometimes fail to intersect.

The issues to be resolved don’t solely lie within policy, legal or technological constraints. It is often social where the connectivity falls down. How do people, who each hold a piece of a public problem, find one another, build trust, and produce outcomes that outlast a ministerial photocall or presidential term? The EU and the Irish Government have invested heavily in the building blocks that are needed for this journey. The digital identity wallets, data spaces and cloud platforms already exist.

What is missing is the right people coming together from different corners, knowing how to assemble these blocks in the right way.

Practitioners who have the ability and mindset to move between a Brussels regulation and a rural county council’s operating reality, without treating the two as separate jobs.

Ireland’s role in this during its EU presidency is reflected in a new initiative that will gather the necessary stakeholders to generate those collective solutions for the next phase of Europe’s digital public services roadmap.

To break the roadblocks and unlock the capabilities that can advance these future services, we need to first go back though to an age-old practice. Before internet technology, quantum computing or artificial intelligence were even imagined, Ireland had meitheal.

This was among our oldest social networks and was based on reciprocity, trust and shared responsibilities. Its approach was replicated in similiar forms in different countries: Norway’s dugnad, Finland’s talkoot, Lithuania’s talka, Hungary’s kaláka and the Balkan moba.

Each European tradition reflects the same civic principle that complex problems can be solved when communities pool effort, skills and responsibility. It activated to do work that no single person or household could manage alone.

The main rule being that help given would be returned. This created a social infrastructure and self-enforcing system for dedicating skills exactly when and where they were needed. That practice and principle may be what is needed now to push forward on Ireland and Europe’s digital public services programme.

On November 19th and 20th, Ireland will hold the first Meitheal Digiteach that will bring policy makers, community groups, data designers, delivery practitioners, architects and engineers into the same room to work through the shared challenges, while looking to create practical solutions and connect the diverging tracks on the new Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) rails.

The gathering will not work like a regular conference with the usual panel discussions, keynote addresses and firesides or roundtables. This will be a hands-on exercise for participants with no hierarchy and no spectators.

It is due to be held at a fitting location within the Drogheda Civic Offices which, since its relatively recent refurbishment, now represents a suitable blend of heritage with modern design and functionality. The call is for like-minded citizens and groups to get involved in building the next level of digital public services.

I’d encourage all who have a role to play to join us, as Ireland’s meitheal provides a mechanism that can be passed on to the next custodians of the EU presidency and the subsequent phases of our shared digital public services programme.

Gar Mac Críosta is digital advisor strategy & architecture at the HSE, and co-founder of Meitheal Digiteach 2026

]]>Marc O'Sullivan<![CDATA[What my most embarrassing job interview taught me]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/what-my-most-embarrassing-job-interview-taught-me/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/what-my-most-embarrassing-job-interview-taught-me/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:24:00 +0000The other day, I was chatting with a friend about how we got into journalism when I suddenly remembered my most disastrously embarrassing job interview.

It happened years ago, not long after I arrived in London and spotted an ad for a deputy news magazine editor. The advert was highly detailed. Applicants had to send in an assessment of the publication outlining what worked and what did not, along with compelling cover story ideas.

Having recently edited a national news magazine in Australia, I was full of thoughts. But there was one question in the advert that stumped me. What was my preferred salary?

I asked two other journalists I knew in London, both men, for advice. Each told me to ask for what I had been paid in Sydney, plus more for the abysmal exchange rate and the cost of living in London, which I did.

To my delight, I got an interview. A team of people politely listened as I went on about their magazine, whose editor then took me off to a side room for a further chat. He loved my application, he said, but there was just one thing. How wedded was I to that salary I had mentioned? “Because it’s a lot more than what I’m paid.”

At the time, I was mortified. My face burned. What an idiot I had been to name such an outlandish figure. Why hadn’t I done a better job of researching the going rate for deputy magazine editors?

Today, though, I recall that moment fondly. Women are always being told they cement the gender pay gap by asking for too little in pay negotiations, and there was my younger self, gormlessly doing the opposite.

I also think of how much easier it would have been if that advert had simply listed the salary on offer. That way, I would have known if it was worth my while to apply and everyone else, inside and outside the magazine, would have had a better idea of whether their pay was fair, or if they should demand more. This is, of course, precisely why so many employers do not spell out salaries in public.

For similar reasons, job hunters are often asked to disclose their salary history, even though this is an excellent way to bake in the lower pay endured by so many women, ethnic minorities and others.

Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?

It’s tough to ask for £50,000 for a job, no matter how well qualified you are, if you have just revealed your last role paid £35,000, which it might have if you had been doing the same work at, say, a charity.

Women were told for years to just “lean in” and become savvier negotiators. Thankfully, this approach is fading as research shows the benefits of policies aimed at fixing the practice of negotiations, instead of fixing the women.

This is why the EU has brought in a directive requiring employers to do two things: tell job seekers about starting salaries or pay ranges, and stop asking them about their pay histories. A number of US states already have such measures, which can help to shrink a gender wage gap that averaged 11 per cent across OECD countries in 2023.

The deadline to put the EU directive into national law was June 2026, but unfortunately many countries have yet to get there. They include Germany, the bloc’s largest economy, where Indeed data shows that less than 15 per cent of job advertisements include explicit pay information. That number plunges for sectors such as banking and finance, which typically have far worse gender pay gaps.

No wonder thousands of women are supporting outfits such as Female X Finance, a five-year-old start-up that aims to help boost women’s careers in the financial industry. Its Dutch co-founders just published their second annual survey of the salaries – and bonuses – being paid in investment banking, M&A, private equity and other fields in the UK and the Netherlands.

HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers

How I wish this type of information, and those pay transparency laws, had been around when I answered that magazine advert all those years ago.

If you’re wondering, I never did get the job. It went to an insider, which is probably just as well. I’m sure they did a far better job than I would have done, but I would still like to know how much they were paid. – The Financial Times

]]>rudi_suardi<![CDATA[‘The focus is finding people from Ireland’: The EU’s big ask for new English translators]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/the-focus-is-finding-people-from-ireland-the-eus-big-ask-for-new-english-translators/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/the-focus-is-finding-people-from-ireland-the-eus-big-ask-for-new-english-translators/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000The list of unintended consequences caused by Brexit runs quite long – and reads somewhat smug when compiled on this side of the Irish Sea – but it can be briefly summarised as political upheaval, economic uncertainty and social division.

Aside from the macro-woes, Britain’s formal departure from the European Union in 2020 has also proved a headache for the diplomats and administrators tasked with running EU institutions for more than 450 million citizens.

“We’re constantly getting requests,” says Linda Forde, the head of the European Parliament’s English-language translation unit, as she takes a short break from her duties during a work trip to Dublin.

Draft after draft of legal documents and policy papers arrive in her inbox daily to be distributed among her team of translators and proofreaders – often with same request: “Can you do this for tomorrow? The day after tomorrow?” she says, quoting colleagues based mostly in Brussels, a three-hour train ride away from her office in Luxembourg.

English, while officially of equal status alongside the EU’s 23 other languages, carries more weight than most because of its status as a “pivot language”.

The term is not easily defined, so Forde provides an example: “Legislation comes in Romanian, we translate it into English and then, for example, the Irish unit will translate it from English because they will not be able to translate it from Romanian.”

The parliament’s translation service employs more than 1,100 people. A standard translation unit is made up of about 30 staff members, but the English unit is among the smallest. This is partly because many texts are originally drafted in English and do not require translation, but the unit’s small size is also a product of its time.

Recruiting translators from Britain has been “problematic” since Brexit, Forde says, due to the EU’s policy of employing strictly its own citizens. The only Britons who can bypass this rule are those with dual citizenship from an EU member state.

“With Ireland being the biggest English-speaking country [in the EU], definitely the focus is finding people from Ireland, because they’re native speakers and that’s what we’re looking for,” says Forde, who is from Co Antrim.

Ireland faces ‘significant’ loss of influence in EU institutions due to retirements

The career translator was in Dublin in early October to speak at an outreach event at the European Parliament’s Liaison Office close to Grafton Street, organised as part of the State’s six-month presidency of the Council of the EU.

Between panel discussions and Q&A sessions, the European Parliament’s director general for translation, Valter Mavric, spoke to The Irish Times about the need for Irish-citizen, English-language translators in the institution.

Irish people “are the only ones that actually can apply. Not formally, not officially, but practically”, the Slovenian man, who is also fluent in Italian, says.

“Theoretically, a Slovenian who has excellent English and has maybe studied in an English-speaking country, might be able to apply. But what’s more important with English, for example, is that you translate the laws or communications for citizens of Ireland primarily.

“So you have to know the Irish version of English,” Mavric says. “That’s why it’s very important to have English native speakers from Ireland.”

‘If you want to get a job immediately in Brussels, speak Irish and do a law degree’

They may well be important to have, but are they difficult to get?

“I think there might be many reasons, before I reply to you, whether it’s difficult or not,” he says in the Robert Schuman breakout room, named after the French elder statesman credited for his role in rebuilding postwar Europe.

Irish citizens “don’t want to leave their country”, he notes, “maybe because it’s so beautiful to live here”. High salaries on offer at home don’t help either, he says.

“Still, we do not have many problems with attracting Irish citizens – we have not had, let’s say it like that, so far,” Mavric adds.

However, “the English team is not complete ... because there are still some colleagues from the UK that work there [since] before Brexit and so they have stayed. But of course, someday these colleagues will retire or will leave and we have to think of succession planning already.”

This is what brought him to Dublin: “We are here this week to promote both English and Irish as the two official languages – for me, it is very important to get that message across.”

Both languages face similar challenges in attracting qualified candidates from Ireland to the highly competitive application process called “translator competitions”, which require applicants to prove fluency in three European languages.

Why foreign governments are paying lobbyists to make their case in Brussels

“Deficiency in knowledge of foreign languages” is the main concern, Mavric says.

Data from the European Commission shows the proportion of Irish secondary school students learning two or more foreign languages was the lowest in the EU, at just 5.2 per cent. In 10 countries, such as Finland and Italy, the proportion was more than 90 per cent.

It appears to be an uphill battle for Ireland to reach the heights of trilingualism, but Mavric is optimistic.

“For me, language is always linked to an identity, to a culture, and that’s why it’s so important to include language as the conditions for the European Union, for the European project. Languages, as part of our lives in Europe, are here to stay.”

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3446285/">
   <title>Mbappe entschuldigt sich für Mao-Äußerung</title>
   <description>Mehrere chinesische Sponsoren haben am Dienstag das Ende der Zusammenarbeit mit dem französischen Fußballstar Kylian Mbappe verkündet. Er soll mit Äußerungen über Revolutionsführer Mao Zedong (1893–1976) die Gefühle der Chinesen verletzt haben. Eine Entschuldigung des Real-Madrid-Stürmers ließ nicht lange auf sich warten. Ob China sie auch annimmt, ist offen, die Übertragung von Spielen der spanischen Liga wurde vorerst ausgesetzt.</description>

   <description>Israels Wahlberechtigte „strömen“ zu den Wahllokalen: Bei der ersten Wahl nach dem Überfall der Terrororganisation Hamas am 7. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445128/">
   <title>Minichmayr und das Leben nach dem Tod</title>
   <description>Eine brillante Reflexion über Trauer und Verlust, ein modernes Drama mit schmerzlich-schönen Bildern und einer herausragenden Birgit Minichmayr ist der neue Film der österreichischen Regisseurin Sandra Wollner. Zwischen der Lebensrealität einer alleinerziehenden Mutter in Berlin und einer surrealen Reise nach Teneriffa tun sich Fragen auf, die einen nicht mehr loslassen. „Everytime“ ist einer der besten Filme des Jahres und hatte bei der Viennale seine Österreich-Premiere.</description>

Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries.

Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche. Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.

She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.

Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.

Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.

Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.

Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.

Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026

Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań.

Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average.

Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20.

 

Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.”

Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia.

“I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports.

“We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”.

Debata ministra @Domanski_Andrz i minister @BMWE_ Katherina Reiche podczas IV Polsko-Niemieckiego Forum Gospodarczego.
💬 Powinniśmy skupić się na cenach energii, ale potrzebne jest znacznie bardziej zdecydowane podejście do ochrony rynku europejskiego. I nie chodzi tu tylko o… pic.twitter.com/NVPUjwx7jA

— Ministerstwo Rozwoju i Technologii (@MRiTGOVPL) October 26, 2026

Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry.

The meeting was attended by representatives of 21 EU member states and European Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné. Discussions focused on protecting and strengthening European industry’s competitiveness and economic security amid geopolitical challenges.

“Today, we are facing the consequences of the fact that, in the past, competitiveness was often relegated to second, third or fourth place. Competitiveness took a back seat to other priorities, with the result that European industry now faces serious challenges,” said Domański.

He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition.

]]> Witness testifies Polish president discussed “making money bringing girls” to hotel where they worked 20 years ago https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/27/witness-testifies-polish-president-discussed-making-money-bringing-girls-to-hotel-where-they-worked-20-years-ago/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:07:24 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106063

A former colleague of Polish President Karol Nawrocki from when he worked as a security guard in a hotel two decades ago testified in court that he told her it was possible to “make some extra money by bringing in girls”. She says she saw him escort a woman onto the premises.

The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot.

The court case began in September but, until now, hearings have been held behind closed doors. However, the judge decided that today’s session would be open to the public, with two former colleagues of Nawrocki giving evidence. The president himself is due to appear before the court in January.

🗣️ "Moją automatyczną oceną było, że to prostytutka i alfons."

Nowe zeznania w procesie Karola Nawrockiego z wydawcą Onetu. Przed sądem stanęła była współpracowniczka prezydenta z sopockiego Grand Hotelu. pic.twitter.com/Cn6KyMSjcv

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 27, 2026

In May last year, less than a week before the second round of the election, in which Nawrocki was standing in a run-off against rival Rafał Trzaskowski, Onet, a leading news website, published an article titled “Karol Nawrocki and the secrets of the Grand Hotel”.

It claimed, based on information provided by unnamed former colleagues of the future president, that he had “participated in bringing prostitutes for guests of the Grand Hotel in Sopot while working there as a security guard” almost 20 years earlier.

Onet said that its interlocutors wished to remain anonymous for their own safety, but had expressed their willingness to testify in court if required.

The revelations caused a major scandal, but were vigorously denied by Nawrocki, a conservative candidate aligned with the right-wing opposition, who called them a “pack of lies”. He then went on to narrowly defeat Trzaskowski in the election.

Conservative presidential candidate @NawrockiKn says he will sue news website @onetpl for claims it published today that he procured prostitutes for clients at a luxury hotel when working there as a security guard.

He called the report "a bunch of lies" https://t.co/WZ4rZWfFT1

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 26, 2025

Nawrocki then sued Ringier Axel Springer Polska (RASP), the Polish subsidiary of a German-Swiss media house that owns Onet, demanding an apology. RASP stood by Onet, saying that its reporting was “factual”.

At today’s hearing, one of Onet’s sources, Natasza Geldon, who had worked at the hotel in 2006 and 2007, was questioned. She said that, one evening, she had noticed Nawrocki leading a man and a woman into the hotel, before then taking only the woman into an elevator and returning alone.

This had struck her as unusual, because staff were not supposed to escort guests into the hotel, “let alone take them upstairs” in the lift, said Geldon, quoted by broadcaster TVP.

“When Karol came back downstairs, I asked him what was going on,” continued the witness. “He said it was possible to make some extra money by bringing girls in, and asked if I wanted to join in.”

Geldon refused the offer, telling the court that, “as a young girl, 19 years old, I had the impression that a pimp had been coming in with a prostitute”. However, when asked to confirm if she had seen prostitutes in the hotel, Geldon said: “I don’t know. It’s hard to say. It was just that one incident.”

 

A second witness, Łukasz Franczak, described as a longtime friend of Nawrocki who worked alongside him in security at the Grand Hotel, also gave evidence on Tuesday after being called by Nawrocki’s legal team.

He testified that there had been prostitutes in the hotel. However, he added that he had not heard of any organised operation to supply them to guests; nor had he witnessed Nawrocki procuring prostitutes or discussing payment for them, reported Onet from the hearing.

Franczak’s testimony was welcomed by Nawrocki’s former national security advisor, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, who said that it showed those making claims against the president have no evidence of his involvement in any wrongdoing.

Oni się wszyscy teraz nakręcają jak szaleni, nie czytając tego co sami piszą na własnej stronie… No i dowiedzieli się dzisiaj, że w hotelach bywają prostytutki 🙂

A ja to wszystko czytam na bieżąco, a tam słynny Łukasz z Gdańska, ulubiony świadek-historyk Antka Dudka, i… https://t.co/9sKGZT4PpD

— Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) October 27, 2026

RASP’s lawyers have called for Nawrocki himself to testify in the case. The president’s legal team wanted him to provide his testimony in writing, according to Onet.

But on Tuesday, judge Aleksandra Orzechowska ordered Nawrocki to give testimony directly – either in person or remotely – at the next hearing, which is scheduled for 18 January 2027, reports broadcaster TVN.

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion.

The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections.

Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej

Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.…

— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026

As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges.

Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read.

In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges.

Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”.

 

Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups.

Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison.

In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month.

 

The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher.

Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”.

For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term.

Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it.

Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition.

The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025

Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions.

In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”.

Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%.

If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition.
