Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges.

“Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.”

The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan.

🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego!

✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026

Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development.

“Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”.

In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place.

Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”.

 

Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland.

The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time.

Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA).

The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group.

Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019

The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”.

It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment.

On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware.

Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history.

Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026

Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”.

“The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added.

Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027.

Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline.

Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026

The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion.

But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”.

Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies

Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026

In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour.

Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20.

]]> Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/26/two-thirds-of-poles-support-liberalising-abortion-law-finds-new-poll/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 10:55:05 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105996

Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand.

In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023

The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.

Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026

In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition.

However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law.

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party.

In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health.

 

However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition.

Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear.

Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”.

The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl.

Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland.

One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland.

 

Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years.

In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases.

That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross.

Thousands of family businesses could face being priced out of passing their business down to their offspring should Chancellor John Healey to use his maiden Budget to clamp down on a little-known rule making it easier for firms to transfer ownership.

Treasury officials have been mulling an overhaul of so-called company distribution rules that would make it more attractive for founders to offload their business to private equity than hand it down to the next generation.

One of the options under consideration – making the transfer of a business from one generation to another liable to income tax as opposed to capital gains – has already sparked uproar from entrepreneurs and business owners.

But Chris Etherington, tax partner at RSM, told City AM that the consultation also includes a suite of other proposals that are “much more troubling” than the capital gains tax clampdown. 

One possibility buried in the HMRC plans published in the summer, could see officials dismantle a buyout structure favoured by many retiring entrepreneurs.

Upon retiring, founders’ families rarely have the cash needed to buy their parents out, leading many companies to issue retiring business owners  ‘redeemable preference shares’. 

The share class acts as a bridge, allowing retirees to freeze their financial stake and slowly withdraw capital from the business over time as the firm makes profit. It also allows children to take immediate control of the company.

These deferred repayments are typically treated as parents selling an investment, meaning it is charged as capital gains tax (CGT), between 10 per cent and 24 per cent.

Shifting to dividend tax

But the consultation looked at scrapping this arrangement for staged handovers by no longer recognising the current, real value of the shares being bought back.

Instead, HMRC has proposed capping the returns at the level originally invested by founders when shares were first issued, meaning anything above that baseline will be recognised as an income dividend.

In the majority of cases, the move would cause retirees’ tax bill to nearly double, as higher and additional rate taxpayers will be slapped with dividend taxes of between 35.75 per cent and 39.35 per cent.

On those handing over £1m, the tax bill can swell from £200,000 to roughly £393,00 making it financially unviable for the next generation to pay off their parents without running out of capital or selling the business.

In a response to the consultation, Mark Goddard, tax partner at KPMG, warned that this overhaul could put families at a “disadvantage” to third-parties and ultimately discourage generational ownership.

RSM’s Etherington said that the government is “trying to clamp down” on people who may be trying to take “advantage of the rules to try and get capital gains tax treatment” when it should be income tax, but warned them to be cautious.

“As a government, don’t… throw such a large net over it that you capture innocent scenarios that fundamentally stop businesses from being passed down to the next generation or to third parties in the right way.”

“It could impact management buyouts, it could impact family buyouts, people just wanting to retire. We don’t want to do that. That’s bad for the economy.”

The two-year trap

HMRC is also considering changes to the conditions under which companies can buyback shares from retiring founders.

Under current legislation, businesses can buy back shares through accumulated profit over several years to protect everyday capital, ensuring enough is set aside to pay taxes, suppliers and wages.

But HMRC is debating ending this by introducing a strict two year-cut off time to qualify for capital gains treatment. If a departing founder still holds shares beyond the 24-month window, companies lose the tax break and payments are instead subject to income tax. 

Advisers have warned this leaves businesses highly exposed to supply chain shocks or other problems if they are forced to purchase all shares over the two year window, as it is a much shorter time frame.

Ahead of the Autumn Budget 2026, and the threat of cheaper gherkins for all, Adam Bloodworth on his love for the humble pickled vegetable, which is both delightfully crunchy and a hack to health

My housemate Will has always been the sort of man with impossible levels of fitness. So when I started a new eat-healthier regime, I went to Will with some questions. I didn’t ask how he got muscular (I assumed that would be from lifting weights) – what felt more relatable was to ask him what he was eating. One of the hacks, he said, is gherkins. They have three calories a piece, he told me, beaming, in our kitchen. 

So it was music to my ears when Burnham’s first budget unveiled an unprecedented price-drop for gherkins in the form of a 12 per cent tariff cut for importing them. 

They also have tartness, a light sweetness, and that famously generous crunch. Once the whole gherkin is inserted into your mouth, they require you to eat a bit like a dog, jaw swinging, eyes fixed, to ensure that everything – juice, flesh – is contained. You could cut them in half but where’s the fun in that? These great, cumbersome things are a workout in themselves.

Autumn Budget 2026 and the return of the gherkin

Anyway, try eating a whole jar at once. That’s what I do, on the regular. It’s now it’s become a part of my personality.

There’s no denying that after demolishing a whole jar, I’m tired. Chewing a family’s week-long supply of the vinegary veg is exhausting, as well as embarrassing, but I’d argue it’s worth it in the end.

By the end of demolishing a jar of gherkins, my jaw hurts. It also does something to your brain: all that chewing makes you feel like you’ve eaten lots. It’s nature’s Ozempic.

At this point I should make clear that it is important not to rely fully on gherkins (always consult your doctor etcetera, etcetera) but you can rely a little bit on them. The fact is I was over-eating and gherkins helped me face the mental block of that head-on, and half an hour after blasting through a jar I could more healthily assess the rest of the food I was going to have for dinner, and it would be far less than I would have had if I hadn’t already gobbed the gherkins.

Leathery bad boys

I’ve taken to buying tins of them to eat at my desk. Sometimes the CEO walks past midway through me crunching down on one of the leathery bad boys, the gherkin half sticking out of my mouth. What can you do? I guess this is just my life, now.

Anyway, I’ve managed to lose five or six kilograms and get within a good weight. It’s about to be party season and I’m sure I’ll crumble a bit at those events, where there will presumably not be a ready supply of pickled veg – but I’m sure I won’t crumble as much as I would have done in my pre-gherkin days.

But I don’t want this to just be about a hedonistic man trying to stay on the right side of the tracks. Nor do I want this to be about the Autumn Budget 2026, that great signifier of autumn and the cold. I want this to be about gherkins. Intensely flavourful, humorously shaped, cartoon like in their curvature, they are joyful little misfits, refreshing for the palette and for the soul. We haven’t even talked about cutting them up and putting them in sandwiches, which is such a popular way of eating them that Pret recently experienced a temporary, stressful shortage. 

Indeed my biggest fear is that the new, lower-priced gherkins following the budget might lead to even more shortages. I’ll have to stock up.

Anyway, it’s time to stop writing about gherkins. I have a jar of them to eat before I decide what to have for lunch.

AI has entered the legal world, but rather than making lawyers lazier, it should force them to think harder, writes Alex Fortescue-Webb in today’s Notebook

AI doesn’t have to mean lazier lawyers

Last week the Law Society made it clear that lawyers remain accountable for how juniors use AI. The legal profession is concerned about indiscriminate AI use, understandably given the number of stories of hallucinations that have hit the headlines. A recent HEPI survey found that 94 per cent of undergrads are using AI for assessed work. So when those students become lawyers, they are already familiar with these tools, but how they use them is largely going unchecked.

Clearly, a lot has changed in the last four years. AI tools are now able to competently take on significant amounts of the routine work juniors used to cut their teeth on. That means two things: first, they will have the opportunity to consider strategic issues much earlier in their careers; second, the way they are trained, and their own self-development, will need to evolve.

The first is a huge positive – involvement in the substantive issues of a case, a transaction or indeed any piece of legal work is the reason many students decide to study law in the first place. Their ambitions will now be realised sooner, and their careers are likely to progress faster.

Good training can support this. AI is going to make training much more specific – available in real time or through highly detailed and tailored simulations. At the same time, junior lawyers should treat AI as a thinking partner rather than relying on it – pushing back on its outputs, interrogating reasoning, verifying key sources and, crucially, taking full responsibility for their work.

We also believe that it is going to be critical for future lawyers to start learning how to use AI as a complement to (rather than a replacement for) their own critical thinking – to support that, we’ve expanded our Legal AI Scholars Programme so that students can experiment with Legora while they study.

Linklaters is adopting AI rapidly

The photo was taken at Legal Tech Talk, where I sat down with Sarah Barnard from Linklaters. We talked the room through how Linklaters got lawyers using AI: almost 80 per cent of its partners now use Legora every month – one of the fastest partner adoption ramps either of us has seen. A big part of that was their approach of training a small group of 12 partners, getting them comfortable with the tech before they brought their colleagues up to speed.

Quote of the week

“Always assume positive intent”

Not sure where that came from but it can really change how you interact with people

Mathematical breakthrough

In September, around 10,000 AI agents working in parallel for 88 hours produced a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems set by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Mathematicians have worked on it for decades without success. The proof still needs independent verification, and the Clay Institute waits two years before considering any solution, but it’s a remarkable moment for mathematics that I’ll be following closely.

A book recommendation

Why We Sleep by Matthew Walker is the book I always recommend to people. Walker, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Berkeley, explains what the research tells us about sleep and how it affects almost every part of our health, from memory and learning to mood. It changed how much I prioritise sleep. In a profession where long hours and late nights are often worn as a badge of honour, it makes a convincing case that proper rest is one of the best things you can do for your work.

Alex Fortescue-Webb is head of UK at Legora

Getty’s bankruptcy caps years of damage to editorial photography and freelance livelihoods; its collapse should inspire little sympathy]]>

So Getty Images has filed for bankruptcy. Excuse me while I locate my microscopic mandolin. Oh dear, how sad, never mind. I, for one, will not shed any tears. To misquote Churchill, never have so many photographers owed such a debt of ingratitude to so few. Back in the day we were all shafted by Getty, albeit sometimes unknowingly. 

Getty flew too close to the sun and got burnt – in the process it left a photography industry that’s a shadow of its former self.

Sadly, I’m not blameless. When I was a young picture editor at the Independent and the Independent on Sunday, juggling million-pound budgets while under the cosh of the accountants and the bean counters, Getty offered a solution to my ever-growing problem. It seemed like such a great idea, something so simple that I kicked myself for not thinking of it. A free at the point of delivery monthly contract. No more guessing over reproduction fees or freelance shifts, just a fixed monthly fee. Predictable and budgetable.

An all-you-can-eat Getty binge

Once you had paid, you could binge on the visual delights of all of their photographers and the many agencies they had brought under their vast and terrible umbrella. A veritable buffet of images, a smorgasbord of sports and news. If you had a seat at the table, it was perfect. If not? Well, that was a different story.

The accountants were happy (which meant I was happy) but the freelancers starved. This one bright idea did more to destroy editorial photography than anything before or since, including the advent of AI.

The money fell out of the market, and freelance news photography starved to death. London, once home to a living, breathing, thriving microeconomy of press photographers – an incubator for new talent – died the death of a thousand cuts.

Once it had eaten news photography alive, it moved on to the then very lucrative market of stock photography, buying libraries and agencies with a view to infinite growth, with a fair bit of asset stripping on the way.

There was a time when stock photography made the photographer and the agency good money. It was a symbiotic relationship: the more commercial your images, the more you made, and the more valuable you were to the agency. Top stock photographers were rock stars, and the release of a new stock catalogue had all the pizzazz of a Hollywood Blockbuster (for me, at least). I remember at college in the 1980s, one such stock photography A-lister gave a talk about the money he was making with the legendary stock agency Tony Stone, and how, as long as we shot on fixed lenses (no zooms allowed) and used transparency film, we could share in his success.

I even recall how the auditorium gasped when the strange grey breezeblock-shaped briefcase next to him started ringing. A mobile telephone! He took the call in front of a hall full of awestruck photography students. We were sold. 

The inevitable downfall of a giant

For a while, it seemed there was enough for everyone, but that wasn’t enough for some, and that symbiotic relationship became cancerous. Those monthly stock agency receipt notices became smaller and smaller. The only option was to submit more and more images for less and less money. The laws of scale may have worked in Getty’s favour, but they were economic ruin for photographers.

Thus Getty disrupted and destroyed photographic markets in its vision for infinite growth; in doing so, it conditioned buyers to expect vast quantities of imagery for less money. The maths still worked for them, provided it continued to grow; for the rest of the market, it salted the well.

Getty swallowed competitors until few remained. Once-grand names are now mere footnotes in  photographic history: Telegraph Colour Library, Allsport, Colourific! 

Then AI arrived and scuppered Getty’s plans. How about all the images you can imagine – for the price of one teeny-tiny monthly fee? No matter how fine your fare, if someone opens a stall next door, giving away something very similar, you will eventually go out of business. There was no loyalty left on Fleet Street. And few people were willing to pay for excellence when ‘good enough’ is part of a free buffet. AI has made everyone experts in mediocrity. 

Getty’s response was to bet the farm on a merger with the giant agency Shutterstock. More growth! But that plan failed – Getty walked away from the deal when the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) insisted Shutterstock first sell off its global editorial business including Shutterstock Editorial, Backgrid and Splash. Getty’s fate was sealed.

No one saw it coming; they never do. New technology always disrupts in ways we can’t quite imagine. Think what would happen to Amazon if you could 3D print everything from grommets to ballpoint pens at home for free. Its business model would vanish just like Getty’s.

Getty was a bright star that grew too big too quickly and then imploded, leaving a black hole that sucked editorial photography into oblivion with it. I would say ‘I told you so’ but what’s the point when there’s no one left to listen?

Roe deer move through the grounds, woodpeckers provide the soundtrack, and the staff are warm rather than starchy. Amid the disruption at airports in Saudi Arabia, the limited access through the Strait of Hormuz and the nagging feeling that the world is on the verge of doom, soft power feels increasingly important. But no longer do quiet meetings always take place in the corners of a consulate or mid-way through a state dinner; instead, new ways to influence geopolitics and exert control are being developed – and one of those is sport.

Recent events have shown how football’s geography is so important to its politics – and who stays in the top job – and it is no different when assessing how both rugby league and union are being used in a wider game of battleships within the Indo-Pacific region and beyond. 

Take the Australian government, which has been an underwriter of the Papua New Guinea rugby league entry into the NRL. The PNG Chiefs – interestingly, sponsored by ExxonMobil branch PNG LMG – forms a key cog in a £300m plan by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to keep the island nation within the political sphere of its southern neighbour. 

With three Rugby World Cups – spanning union and league – in four years, Australia is also backing Fiji, Samoa, Tonga through rugby development, while it had involvement in the recent Super Rugby franchise expansion.

Soft power playing part

But why? Because of China and wider actors, of course. China’s Belt and Road initiative is usually associated with Africa but it extends into the Pacific, too. The nation built the Pacific Games Stadium Complex on the Solomon Islands, did similar in Fiji and Samoa, and donated to the Fijian women’s rugby union team last year to celebrate International Women’s Day.

“The South-West Pacific region, sometimes known as Melanesia, is one of the world’s most strategically important trade chokepoints and is therefore an increasingly sensitive territory,” sport and geopolitics scholar Professor Simon Chadwick tells City AM. “It is a maritime gateway that forms a vital part of what is often referred to as the Second Island Chain, making it a crucial buffer zone for Australia’s northern approaches.

“A range of diplomatic instruments is being deployed by these countries which extends to the use of sport. In particular, both countries have been investing in the Melanesian game, indeed interventions by the Australian government now see teams from Papua New Guinea competing in both its union and league competitions.”

But the two main players aren’t the only ones on the pitch. Qatar offered subsidies to the Pacific Islands if it won the right to stage a Rugby World Cup, while also being part of an agreement with the French Rugby Union – alongside China – to develop programmes across the game.

A political pawn

France itself funds rugby programmes in New Caledonia and Wallis and Futuna and has coaching agreements with Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. Japan does similar, while the UK uses the Ministry of Defence and rugby to build relations. The US and UAE also use sports envoy programmes to further their cause.

This helps to explain a potential new NRL franchise partly based in and backed by New Zealand, with home games taking place in the Cook Islands, United States, Tonga and Samoa – the latter is currently seeing government threats to its rugby union programme. And to top it all off, next year’s rugby union World Cup will feature Hong Kong for the first time, except in 2027 they’ll play as Hong Kong China.

“The region is rich in deposits of gold, copper, nickel and liquified natural gas,” Chadwick added. “All of which makes the region a key area for power projection by the likes of Australia and China, which compete for power and influence there. 

“Sport clearly and increasingly plays a crucial role in building relations, extending influence and projecting soft power.”

Investing in sport is always a popular vote winner at home, but internationally it is a crucial part of developing relationships with new friends, or shoring up backing against political enemies. Who said sport and politics aren’t intertwined?

Children may be being given SpaceX shares over in the States, but UK pension reforms means Brits can access superstar companies through their savings, writes Ian Cornelius

News arrived last week that Elon Musk will give every American child a share in SpaceX. It comes days after Anthropic, the frontier AI firm, announced plans for five per cent of its shares to be placed in a ‘public benefit’ fund. OpenAI, its competitor, reportedly floated a similar proposal in July.

Whatever you might think about the necessity or underlying motivations of these plans, it’s worth pausing on why they’re so eye-catching in today’s market.

Consider this: When Microsoft listed in 1986, it was worth less than a billion dollars. Anyone with a modest shareholding came along for the extraordinary ride that followed. You could say it grew ‘in public’.

By contrast, early growth in today’s superstar companies is the reserve of billionaires, sovereign wealth funds, various endowments and the sort of global-scale pension funds that historically the UK has largely lacked. Today’s Microsofts can stay private for a lot longer. The value that these companies reach over a handful of years has already been captured, to the benefit of wealthy early investors. This means that, for the most part, ordinary British savers are left out.

In this era of dominant private markets, UK pension funds must find a way for British workers and savers to access the widest possible range of investments. That might be the chance of catching the next superstar, or diversifying market risk through ‘boring’ but stable assets like housing and infrastructure. This is how the richest ensure their wealth increases no matter what: they combine a strategy of ‘limited downside/unlimited upside’ with stable income regardless of what goes on in public markets. The same approach should be available to everyone, but it gets harder as so much value is kept behind closed doors.

How pension reforms are helping Brits

This week, the ABI published the latest figures on progress towards the pension industry’s Mansion House commitments. Signatories committed 10 per cent of their portfolios to be invested in private markets, half of which will be invested in the UK. The figures from the ABI show it is possible: more than £11bn has been invested so far in UK private markets, giving pension fund members access to what is otherwise off-limits.

For example, Nest, where I work, is an investor in the British startup Wayve, which is bringing its self-driving cars to London, one of the world’s first cities to host the new tech. 

We’re also in on companies like Citation, a tech firm in the North West providing compliance services to 110,000 customers, and 9fin, a British fintech startup valued at $1.3bn. In total, we have committed £3bn to unlisted equities – around five per cent of our portfolio – one in every five pounds of which is invested in the UK.

All three are examples of the UK’s world-class tech ecosystem, and they sit alongside other great firms, homes and infrastructure in Britain and beyond whose returns our members might never access without the reach that their pension fund provides.

I’m especially proud of the fact that our scale has enabled us to do this on our terms: we do not pay performance fees – all of the upside goes to our members. Investing on their own terms is another thing that the wealthy get access to, but that we now offer to savers by merit of our scale, positioning and thoughtful approach.

But what matters to pension funds like us is the new opportunity and unique access it gives to our members. They won’t have to wait for a billionaire to give away shares in Wayve and 9fin and Citation, or in thousands of others like them – they’re already bought in.

Despite the professional services sector dodging tax hikes on LLPs in last year’s Budget, it remains unclear whether Chancellor John Healey will impose tax changes this time round, but Rosie Harris-Davison writes that experts have warned against any tax burdens on the sector.

In the lead-up to last year’s Budget, whispers circulated for weeks that Rachel Reeves was considering taxing LLP firms. However, after sector-wide lobbying against the move, the former Chancellor rolled back the plans.

The LLP model came into force over 25 years ago and is used by many firms across the professional services industry, including law firms, accountancy firms, and some doctors. It is a structure in which members, known as partners, invest their own capital, take on the risk, and, in return, do not pay corporate tax on their profits.

Private client tax partner at RSM, Chris Etherington, told City AM that if tax hikes are imposed on LLPs in the upcoming Budget, it “would lead to some competition issues” among firms and disruption to the wider LLP market.

“You’ve got some large law firms which are not set up as LLPs are just general partnerships. If you’re taxing one more, you’re distorting the market slightly,” Etherington said. He added that the move risks the market becoming more disrupted as firms “could just move offshore, frankly.”

In terms of the impact of LLP tax hikes on the firms’ equity partners, Etherington said it “will have a similar impact to a rising corporation tax”, but it will be equivalent to income tax hitting their personal taxes, and have “a knock-on effect potentially” for customers, employees, and business investment.

While risking their own capital and not benefiting from the protections available to employees at LLPs, partners already face tax rates close to 50 per cent, meaning they will bear a heavy brunt of any tax on the firms.

The professional and business services sector is an economic engine for Britain, and in 2025, it contributed £335bn to the UK economy and is one of the UK’s largest employers.

Sean Drury, Head of tax at Blick Rothenberg, told City AM the government “should be wary” of imposing tax on LLPs as the partnership structure “has been effective in attracting professional and financial services organisations to the UK.”

“Similar structures are available elsewhere, so I am unsure that the government is looking for an outcome which would disincentivise organisations to base or invest in the UK where they have other locations for the investment,” Drury said.

Budget may have tweaks rather than shocks

Alexandra Ueno-Park, partner at Haynes Boone, told City AM that despite nothing being confirmed yet in the upcoming Budget, she expects it to “bring tweaks rather than shocks”, but firms would “be wise to model the potential cost now.”

Back in July, the Supreme Court reignited anxieties over possible tax hikes for LLPs after billionaire and founder of hedge fund, BlueCrest Capital Management, Michael Platt, lost a £200m tax battle with HMRC after the court rejected the firm’s argument that its partners were technically self-employed and therefore not subject to the same income tax and national insurance as normal employees.

“After years of upheaval over salaried member rules, Supreme Court litigation and carried interest reforms, professional services need one thing above all: stability. If change is coming, it should come only after a full and proper consultation,” Ueno-Park said.

Sarah Curzon, tax partner at MHA, told City AM any tax changes to the LLP model “could have significant consequences for the UK professional services sector.”

“Professional services is an important UK growth sector and one in which the UK has a strong international position,” Curzon said. “With employment costs having increased and firms also needing to make substantial investment in technology, data and AI, further increases in the tax cost of operating an LLP could add to those pressures.”

Curzon added that if any tax changes “significantly alter the relative tax position of LLPs”, she anticipates that firms will “review whether the LLP remains the most appropriate structure.”

Legal sector sounds alarm

Last year, the legal sector sounded the alarm over Reeves’ proposal, with industry bodies such as the Law Society demanding “absolute clarity” that the plans had been quashed.

Colin Passmore, Chairman of the City of London Law Society (CLLS), echoed the same concerns ahead of this year’s Budget.

“Any return of last year’s proposals to extend national insurance to LLP partners would be both unfair and damaging to growth. LLPs are taxed in the same way as other partnerships, so there is no loophole to close,” Passmore told City AM.

Passmore said any changes would “create new distortions rather than correct an existing one.”

“Those distortions would push firms to restructure how they pay and organise their partners, or to move work to competing centres such as New York, Singapore and the Gulf,” Passmore said.

“That would undermine one of the UK’s most successful exports at precisely the moment the government is looking to the private sector for growth. We fully support a fair tax system, which is why a change of this significance should only follow proper consultation with the profession,” he added.

When approached for a comment, a Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

That should give the Chancellor pause for thought. Policies that discourage investment and hiring risk making his fiscal challenge harder, not easier. This Budget is an opportunity to stop adding to those pressures and give businesses the breathing space they need to grow. 

The Chancellor should start by ruling out further increases in employment taxes during this Parliament and freezing the business rates multiplier for 2027/28, while committing to wider reform of a system that too often penalises expansion. 

Reducing costs is only part of the answer. Businesses also need confidence that the economic and tax environment will remain stable enough for them to plan ahead. Greater clarity over the government’s fiscal rules, including what constitutes “current budget balance”, would help avoid unwelcome surprises for markets. There is also much the government could do to make running a business easier. Improving HMRC’s performance would reduce the delays and unnecessary costs businesses face, while expanding the Growth Guarantee Scheme would help smaller firms access the finance they need to invest and grow. 

None of this requires the Chancellor to abandon fiscal discipline. It means recognising that stronger businesses and healthier public finances go hand in hand. Yet the problems facing British business cannot be solved through one Budget alone. Britain’s increasingly complex tax system is already holding back growth and risks becoming unfit for the economy of the future without fundamental reform. 

Successive Budgets have added rules, thresholds and reliefs, often without enough consideration of how they fit together. The result is one of the world’s most complex tax codes, one that has grown more than fourteenfold over the past 50 years.  

At the same time, the economy our tax system needs to support is changing rapidly. AI, shifting demographics and weak productivity growth raise difficult questions about where future tax revenues will come from and how we fund public services. 

We cannot assume that a tax system built up through decades of piecemeal changes will be fit for an economy undergoing profound transformation. That is why we have established the Future of Tax Commission, an independent body chaired by former Treasury Minister Mark Hoban which begins its two-year programme of work in January 2027, to examine what a better tax system should look like and how we might get there. 

This Budget can give businesses room to breathe. But securing Britain’s long-term prosperity means looking beyond individual Budgets and asking how our tax system can better support growth and sustainable public finances. At ICAEW, we have begun that work. I want government, businesses and policymakers to be part of it. We have an opportunity to think seriously about the tax system Britain will need in the decades ahead, and we should not waste it.

City grandees have called on the government to revive “animal spirits” in London’s capital markets and accelerate regulatory reform on the anniversary of the Big Bang.

Industry leaders told City AM the City has enjoyed decades of success since the sweeping deregulation of the Square Mile in 1986 but Britain’s financial services industry is now facing existential threats in the form of a downturn in public equity investment and a flight of firms away from the London Stock Exchange.

“No international financial center has a God-given right to success, and complacency is the single most dangerous thing that any international financial centre can indulge,” Miles Celic, chief executive of TheCityUK, told City AM.

He added the Big Bang does not need to be “followed by a Big Bang 2.0 and then in another 40 years a Big Bang 3.0” and reform of the UK’s capital market should instead be viewed as “a journey”.

Spearheaded by Margaret Thatcher’s government on October 27 1986, the Big Bang dismantled fixed commissions, ended the divide between brokers and jobbers, and opened London’s trading floors to foreign banks and screen-based electronic dealing.

Since taking power in 2024, Labour has promised to reinvigorate the City through scrapping burdensome regulation. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves handed watchdogs a secondary growth objective that required them to consider the international competitiveness of the UK alongside their core roles of stability. 

“Regulators have done a lot to improve the environment and improve the opportunity for companies to list in the UK,” Steven Fine, chief executive of Peel Hunt, said. 

“What we need now is a big bang on the capital side to reignite the City’s animal spirits. We need to incentivise domestic investors to back UK listed stocks and to stop rewarding them for investing overseas.”

Stacey Parsons, managing director at Retail Book, said: “The piece of the puzzle that’s now needed is confidence and stability. Less policy and more practice. We need to start treating UK capital markets as national infrastructure.” 

The London Stock Exchange has faced a testing few years with a drought of new IPOs and a flurry of delistings and foreign takeovers. Since the start of 2023 there have been 166 bids for firms with a price tag over £100m with the collective value topping £180bn. This is compared to just 11 IPOs above £100m for a total value of £6bn.

“Forty years on from the Big Bang, the London Stock Exchange continues to evolve, but our purpose remains the same: supporting ambitious companies and the investors who back them,” Julia Hoggett, chief executive of the London Stock Exchange, said.

“That continuous innovation is vital to ensuring that our markets are able to unlock the capital that delivers what matters – investment in businesses, jobs and growth across the country.”

In the 2025 Budget, Reeves launched a stamp duty holiday, removing the 0.5 per cent levy on UK stocks for newly-listed companies in their first three years of trading. But industry has continued to urge the government to go further and boost tax incentives to invest. 

Their warnings come ahead of a John Healey’s maiden Budget on Wednesday in which he is expected to hit the UK’s banking sector with higher taxes. He has reportedly ruled out hiking capital gains tax over fears it would hammer investment into the UK.

    Ahead of the upcoming Budget, the Debt Management Office’s financing choices and shifting market demands pose a critical test for government borrowing stability, says Helen Thomas

    Another year, another Budget. The same party remains in charge, but a fresh cast of characters will deliver it, bringing fresh uncertainty over the government’s economic direction. For John Healey, the first Chancellor to bear that surname since Denis Healey’s unfortunate encounter with the IMF in 1976, the incentive to “do no harm” is particularly strong.

    Yet the officials whose announcements could matter most to financial markets on Wednesday sit a short distance from Downing Street, at 21 Mincing Lane. The Debt Management Office will update the government’s financing plans for this financial year, alongside projections of the demands to come.

    This is consequential small print. Ministers decide how much to tax and spend but it is the DMO who arranges the borrowing that makes those decisions possible. Working within the Treasury’s remit, it manages the mix of gilts, their maturities and the timetable of auctions. Its choices help determine how readily the government can find buyers, and how much refinancing risk taxpayers carry.

    Recently, that has meant retreating from the long end of the market. Bonds offering certainty over several decades once found natural buyers among pension funds. As that demand has diminished, selling long-dated debt has become more challenging.

    The latest Reuters poll of gilt dealers suggests bonds maturing in more than 15 years will account for just around 7 per cent of issuance, a significant fall from more than 30 per cent just five years ago. The same dealers expect the net contribution from Treasury bills to double from £5bn to £10bn this year.

    Trade-offs

    There is a trade-off. Shorter borrowing can match investor appetite today but must be refinanced sooner. The government exchanges some immediate funding pressure for greater exposure to whatever interest rates prevail when the debt comes due. If inflation proves stubborn, that can become an expensive bargain.

    September offered a reminder of how quickly the environment can change. Ten-year US Treasury yields recorded their biggest monthly rise since September 2022, the month of Britain’s mini-Budget crisis. The forces unsettling bond markets now extend far beyond Westminster.

    Governments have substantial deficits to finance and old debt to replace. France plans €340bn of medium- and long-term issuance next year, net of buybacks, up from €310bn this year. Its debt agency attributes much of the increased financing requirement to maturing bonds issued through the pandemic and energy crises. Yesterday’s emergency borrowing is becoming tomorrow’s refinancing problem.

    Germany’s planned securities issuance this year exceeds €512bn, roughly a fifth above last year and two-and-a-half times its pre-pandemic level. Even Europe’s benchmark borrower is surpassing the volumes seen during the pandemic and energy crises, as defence and infrastructure spending add to its financing demands.

    Nor do governments have the market to themselves. The hyperscalers are financing data centres, chips and power supplies on a scale that is changing corporate bond markets. According to Goldman Sachs, their bond issuance to date this year has already doubled from last year’s $108bn. Companies once able to finance their ambitions from abundant cash flows are becoming substantial competitors for investors’ capital.

    The appetite extends into riskier credit. SoftBank hit a record when they raised $11.1bn in a high-yield bond offering in September; within a week, Paramount Skydance’s junk-bond deal had eclipsed this, reaching approximately $12.4bn. These are formidable transactions even before the wider borrowing needed to finance acquisitions and artificial intelligence is counted.

    Sovereign and corporate bonds are not interchangeable. But investors can compare their returns, adjust allocations and demand better compensation for committing capital. Higher yields attract buyers but they also create an incentive to wait if still higher yields seem likely. Nobody wants to catch a falling knife.

    This is where inflation could make already difficult fiscal arithmetic worse. Another Middle East energy shock would squeeze real incomes and growth while increasing pressure for government support. Inflation-linked debt becomes more expensive; benefits and pensions can rise; persistent price pressures can keep interest rates higher. As cheap debt matures, refinancing it at higher yields adds to the interest bill.

    Inflation can also lift nominal tax receipts and erode the real value of fixed-rate debt. But a supply shock brings no guarantee that those gains will outweigh the costs. If interest spending increases borrowing, and that additional borrowing itself attracts higher yields, the adjustment becomes progressively harder.

    Healey therefore needs Wednesday’s financing numbers to reassure the market. Dealers expect full-year gross gilt sales to rise by £3.4bn to £249.6bn; for next year they expect the gross financing requirement, before contributions such as NS&I, to reach roughly £334bn, £27bn above March’s projection. Lower-than-expected figures could usher in a gilt relief rally. Markets, after all, are still places where buyers and sellers meet: less debt for investors to absorb can mean higher prices. For all the attention paid to fiscal headroom, it rests on forecasts and spending promises that may never survive contact with political reality. The DMO’s issuance plans can also change, but they provide a much more concrete guide to what investors will actually be asked to finance.

    A relief rally would give Healey a successful first Budget and Burnham another reason to consider an early election. But the government would still have to refinance its debts, compete with other borrowers and absorb the cost of any renewed inflation shock. Shortening maturities brings those tests around more often. Wednesday may deliver a reassuring verdict from the bond market; the government’s growing dependence on its next verdict will remain.

    Helen Thomas is founder and CEO of Blonde Money
