“We are a service company. Service-as-a-software: it means our software absorbs the operational complexity – the admin, the workflows, the manual steps – so our talents can spend their time on what actually matters: the relationship,” added Eduardo.

The acquisition of pro-van comes weeks after Naboo unveiled a new brand identity in October and opened its first Asia-Pacific office in Singapore. The company has raised €90 million ($100 million) in the past three years) and now aims to exceed €900 million ($1 billion) in business volume by 2027.

]]> Cortas, a Copenhagen-based PropTech startup building what it calls an entirely new operating model for property management, has raised €1.47 million in pre-Seed funding.

The round was led by PSV Tech, which has backed Nordic companies for more than two decades and includes Lunar, Helloflow and Spektr in its portfolio. The round also saw participation from JRNY Capital and a cohort of seasoned tech entrepreneurs, including founders of Danish FinTech Flatpay and EV-charging platform Spirii.

“Cortas won’t be the only company trying to rethink property management. What matters to us is that we believe this team has the potential to succeed. Christian and Frederik combine tremendous drive and ability to execute with first-hand experience from the property investor’s side. They have the industry insight and the right network to deliver on their ambition of serving large, demanding property investors from day one,” said Christian Dalsgaard, Investment Manager, PSV Tech.

The PropTech startup was founded by Christian Pind Schmidt and Frederik Buchardt, both alumni of Thylander Group, one of Denmark’s major real estate investors. During their time at Thylander Group, the founders gained direct exposure to the fragmented systems and cumbersome workflows that long defined the property management sector, and they set out to change that.

Unlike conventional approaches that layer technology on top of existing solutions, Cortas is built on the conviction that property management and the software powering it should come from the same company. Its founders say these two functions have traditionally been provided separately.

Cortas is bringing these two functions under one roof, developing its own tools while using them to manage clients’ properties. This approach, they argue, will lead to a materially better experience for both owners and tenants.

The startup is targeting Denmark as its launch market, where the property management sector is estimated to be worth between €270 million and €400 million annually. The market is dominated by established players such as DEAS, Newest and CEJ, which account for more than a third of the market. The global market for property management, meanwhile, is valued at more than €400 billion.

As Dalsgaard said, Cortas won’t be the only company aiming to transform the property management sector, but the distinction lies in how it goes about it. The company describes itself as AI-native, but it is also quick to push back against the idea of AI-fication of everything.

“We don’t see using AI as a strategy in itself. It is an exciting technology because it allows us to rethink the entire property management business model from the ground up. But, like any other technology, AI has to earn its place by creating real value for our customers,” said Pind Schmidt, co-founder and CEO of Cortas.

Buchardt, co-founder and COO of Cortas, argues that the company will be a service-first PropTech startup rather than tech-first. “We don’t start by asking where we can implement AI. We start by asking how to provide the best possible property management service. Sometimes AI is the right solution. Elsewhere, it’s conventional automation, better processes or skilled people. The result matters, not which technology we can apply,” he said.

This selective implementation of AI also extends to how Cortas works with the company, focused on automating administrative tasks to free employees for work where human judgment, specialist knowledge, and relationships are most valuable.

Since June, Cortas has built a new operating model and software and signed its first property-investor customers. With the pre-Seed capital, the startup plans to further develop its technology platform, expand its team, and position itself as a credible alternative to the established names currently dominating the Danish property management market.

]]> Part one was about strategy: the “why” behind PR, which stakeholders to chase, how to move them, and which media channels to pursue. You have the map, but now you need to understand the territory and how to move effectively inside of it.

Three practical considerations remain before you are ready to pitch: what actually earns a journalist’s attention, which activities are worth the effort, and how to conduct yourself effectively and ethically.

Newsworthiness

So what makes it to the media? Can you pitch anything you want? Not really. To determine what gets covered and what doesn’t, it helps to understand the concept of newsworthiness. If something is newsworthy, it is important and interesting enough to be covered in the media (whether it’s a news announcement or not).

The “gatekeepers” mentioned in the last piece all have their own perceptions of what is and isn’t newsworthy. Newsworthiness varies by outlet, by person, and changes with time. We can break it down into five main components.

Timeliness comes first and can be determined in two ways: short-term and long-term. Short-term timeliness is controllable, as the source decides when newsworthy information, such as funding announcements, is released to the media and typically covered that same day. Long-term timeliness, however, depends on external developments beyond the source’s control, such as breaking news, regulatory changes, or cultural trends that align with the current zeitgeist.

The second factor is impact. And when we say impact, we mean scale. Some stories make it based on sheer size because they involve staggering revenue, eye-watering funding rounds, or skyrocketing headcount. Bigger numbers make bigger stories, which explains why funding rounds remain such reliable triggers. They arrive with a figure and a set of backers that together signal validation. To be clear, a non-funding-related action that has an outsize effect on the industry, society or a human life, is equally newsworthy. A case study of new technology that saved a person’s life, which would have not been otherwise possible, is also a good example of impact.

Geography matters more than founders expect. A national desk may wave aside what a local or regional outlet would treat as a genuine event, and trade titles care about their own patch above all else. Starting close to home is usually the easiest way in, and it is the lever most startups overlook. Wanting US or UK hits as a small startup in mainland Europe is usually wishful thinking, but European startup outlets may have better openings.

Name recognition goes a long way. A well-known investor, a notable advisor, or a marquee client can elevate an entire story by lending credibility. A journalist who would pass on an unknown startup will often look twice when a familiar name is involved. “Celebrity” counts, especially if you have a real celebrity, like when the legal AI platform Legora hired the aptly-named Jude Law as a spokesperson.

Conflict is the most volatile of the five factors. Newsrooms are drawn to tension and disagreement, but picking fights can backfire on young companies trying to build goodwill. There are exceptions, mostly in the form of a clear, defensible stance on the trajectory of your industry. (Mudslinging at competitors is not something wise for early stage startups to do.) Even so, this is a rare exception, not a strategy.

Before pitching anything, look hard at your own company, technology, product and people, and be objective about genuine newsworthiness versus merely interesting to you. Study your target channels, and what they cover. What do they find newsworthy? That will show you what is newsworthy, to whom, and where.

Activity tracks

Across those channels, think in terms of sustained activities rather than one-off hits. Three tracks are worth knowing.

News is the obvious and easiest one. For an early startup, a funding announcement is usually the most valuable of all. It carries a number and a set of named backers, which together read as validation you cannot otherwise claim alone. Milestones such as a new product launch, a marquee customer, a new market, a hire senior enough to signal intent work similarly, but may be newsworthy only in trade and smaller media. For news, journalists tend to appreciate a well-written, factual press release. Don’t believe those that say the press release is dead!

Thought leadership is the second track, and the most misunderstood. It’s not shameless self-promotion, just like PR isn’t. It’s a contribution to the industry and community by sharing a point of view, insight or constructive criticism about your field. It’s your contribution to a larger conversation. In PR, the value of that contribution needs to be substantial enough to warrant a third-party media platform, which in turn lends you a higher level of credibility. Thought leadership comes in many forms, but op-eds, podcasts and speaking slots are the most common. 

Profiling is the third. It can take the form of Q&As, features and company or executive profiles that give a face and human identity to a business. Sometimes labelled “slots” or “series“, these are out there for the taking once you have traction, so understand which outlets and journalists do them, what truly interests them, and pitch them.

Not everyone has frequent newsworthy items or time for thought leadership. But ideally, you’ll have a good enough mix. Once you’re solid in your PR journey, more activity tracks become available, but that’s for another time.

Keep it human

A last word, because this is where the whole thing can come undone. Everything rests on real people trusting real people. The temptation to automate the human away is strong and growing. A PR agency was recently caught pitching journalists using a roster of fake, AI-generated PR pros, all without telling clients. Journalists notice, and they do not forgive it.

A similar logic applies to a number of other lazy shortcuts: blasting emails without checking relevance, fully AI-written pitches, etc. It wastes journalists’ time and weakens your credibility, and it is the quickest way to undo months of careful work. Use AI the way good journalists do. Follow them and see what they think about AI, you’ll find they appreciate it for research, analysing notes and internal documents and a number of other secondary tasks. This is a very fluid area, so stay up to date.

Your PR methodology

PR is not rocket science, but few take the time to learn it. This article aims to be less a set of tactics than a practical framework to help founders think about PR without overcomplicating it.

A reputation doesn’t rest on one headline but many trusted sources over time that tell a consistent story about who you are. Build that, and the big title you always wanted might eventually come to you. But never mistake the foundation for the cherry on top.

]]> A mystery object spotted by the crew of a British Airways flight to New York has been classified as a serious air safety incident after passing within an estimated 50ft of the aircraft shortly after take-off from Heathrow.

The aircraft was climbing through 5,800 feet near Guildford, Surrey, when the crew spotted what appeared to be a silver, metallic object travelling in the opposite direction. They described it as reflective and about the “size of four toasters”. The pilots thought it might be a drone. 

The UK Airprox Board investigated the report in September and gave it a Category A rating, meaning there had been a serious risk of collision. The case record describes the object as being “too close for comfort.”

British Airways addresses the UFO sighting

The crew reported the sighting to air traffic control at around 12:08 UTC. The incident did not require evasive action, and the flight continued to New York, where it landed on schedule.

A British Airways spokesperson told The Independent: “We take matters such as these extremely seriously, and our pilots report these incidents so authorities can investigate them and take appropriate action.”

The Airprox Board considered the report at its September meeting, recording it as case 2026127. Investigators could not find matching radar contact for the object, and were unable to identify it.

More unidentified objects reported near UK airports

The Airprox Board’s September 2026 records contain other reports of unidentified flying objects spotted near passenger aircraft.

On 21 June, an Airbus A320 crew departing Heathrow saw a large object they believed could be a drone, although investigators could not confirm.

There were also sightings reported by Boeing 787 crews flying near Rochdale and Birmingham.

A UFO is simply an object in the sky that has not been identified. It does not imply that the flying object is of extraterrestrial origin. Some past sightings have been explained as aircraft, balloons, satellites or natural phenomena. 

The UK National Archives holds records of UFO sightings reported to the Ministry of Defence, including many accounts from airline pilots.

British Airways pilots have reported UFO sightings before

In January 1995, pilots aboard a BA Boeing 737 flying from Milan to Manchester reported seeing a wedge-shaped object with lights pass near their aircraft.

The 737 was descending through 4,000 feet when the object appeared on its right-hand side. The first officer reportedly ducked as it went past.

The Civil Aviation Authority’s Joint Airmiss Working Group investigated the sighting but could not explain it. Ministry of Defence records released later showed that military aircraft had been ruled out. The MOD found no evidence of a threat to UK air defences.

Another BA crew reported an unusual sighting over Ireland on 9 November 2018. The pilots were flying a Boeing 787 from Montreal to Heathrow on flight BA94 when they spotted a bright object moving rapidly near their aircraft.

]]> Electra Aero has taken another step toward its vision for airport-independent regional aviation after its EL2 hybrid-electric demonstrator landed and took off from a Lower Manhattan heliport.

The demonstration took place on 26 October at Downtown Skyport, a waterfront facility operated by Skyports Infrastructure.

Electra believes the event marked the first time a conventional fixed-wing aircraft without vertical take-off capability had landed at the heliport.

The flight formed part of the company’s Life Beyond Runways programme, which aims to demonstrate how aircraft capable of operating within extremely short distances could open new regional routes without requiring conventional airport runways.

The technology is intended to underpin Electra’s larger EL9, a nine-passenger aircraft the company hopes to introduce into commercial service around 2030.

Blown-lift technology enables ultra-short operations

Electra’s EL2 Goldfinch is a two-seat technology demonstrator designed to test the company’s approach to ultra-short take-off and landing (USTOL).

Its defining feature is blown-lift technology, which directs airflow from electrically driven propellers over the wings and large flaps.

This increases lift at low airspeeds, allowing the aircraft to become airborne after a much shorter ground roll than a conventional aeroplane would require.

Once airborne and established in cruise, the aircraft can retract its flaps and transition to normal fixed-wing flight.

Electra’s target for the production-oriented EL9 is a take-off and landing ground roll of approximately 150 feet (46 metres). That could enable operations from suitably prepared heliports and other confined locations that would be unsuitable for most conventional aircraft.

A different approach to regional travel

Electra calls its proposed operating model ‘Direct Aviation’. Rather than concentrating regional services around major airports, the concept envisages flights connecting passengers through a distributed network of smaller departure and arrival points.

Potential locations include heliports, small airfields, waterfront facilities, fields and other suitable sites. The objective is to reduce the time passengers spend travelling to airports and navigating busy terminals.

According to Electra’s own market analysis, its proposed approach could save travellers approximately three hours and 45 minutes on journeys between New York and Boston, three hours and 30 minutes between New York and Washington, D.C., and 45 minutes between New York and Philadelphia.

These figures are company estimates, rather than demonstrated savings from an operating passenger service.

For Downtown Skyport, the demonstration illustrates how existing helicopter facilities might eventually accommodate additional forms of regional transport.

Robbie Ladov, Skyports Infrastructure’s general manager for US heliports and vertiports, said the aircraft could expand the facility’s potential connections beyond conventional helicopter journeys.

Electra chief executive Marc Allen similarly emphasised the possibility of using existing infrastructure instead of constructing new runways.

EL9 development and certification

The EL2 is a technology demonstrator, while the larger EL9 is intended to become Electra’s commercial product.

The planned EL9 will accommodate up to nine passengers and use eight electric motors powered by a hybrid-electric system incorporating batteries and a turbine-driven generator.

The generator is designed to supply electricity during flight and support battery recharging.

Electra has published a projected cruise speed of 175 knots and a maximum ferry range of 1,100 nautical miles with reserves.

Its certification announcement also describes the aircraft as being designed for routes of up to 330 nautical miles, illustrating the distinction between maximum ferry capability and intended passenger operations.

In July 2026, Electra announced that the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had established the EL9’s certification basis, an important early step in the aircraft’s type-certification programme.

The company is targeting a first flight in late 2027 or early 2028, with commercial entry into service planned for 2030.

Electra reports more than 2,200 letters of intent from over 60 commercial customers, including airlines and helicopter operators. It also has relationships with US government customers, including the Air Force, Army, Navy and NASA.

Demonstration success is only the beginning

Despite the progress, the Manhattan flight does not by itself establish that regular passenger operations from heliports are commercially or operationally ready. The EL9 must still progress through development, testing and certification.

Operators will also need suitable infrastructure, regulatory approvals and viable routes before the concept can become a routine transport option.

Nevertheless, the demonstration highlights an alternative approach to regional aviation: using fixed-wing efficiency while reducing dependence on conventional runways.

If Electra can translate its demonstrator’s performance into a certified passenger aircraft, existing urban heliports and other compact sites could become useful links in a broader regional transport network.

]]> Space mirror startup faces criticism over plans to bring sunlight to Earth at night https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/reflect-orbital-space-mirror-satellite-controversy/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:39:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54581 Reflect Orbital faces mounting opposition after a California lighting demonstration, as scientists question its plans to reflect sunlight from orbit.

]]> A California startup planning to reflect sunlight from orbit onto Earth after dark is facing mounting criticism from scientists, environmental groups and local residents, following a ground demonstration that illuminated part of the California desert at night.

Reflect Orbital, which hopes to deploy thousands of mirror-equipped satellites to provide sunlight on demand, has defended its technology as a potential tool for emergency responders and solar power operators. Critics warn that deliberately lighting the night sky could disrupt wildlife, interfere with astronomy and expose communities to illumination they never requested.

The controversy intensified after the company staged a demonstration near Lone Pine, California, earlier this month, using powerful ground-based lights to simulate the effect of sunlight reflected from space.

According to The Guardian, which reported the demonstration on October 26, some residents were startled by the unexpected illumination. One described the lights as “blinding”.

The demonstration was conducted using equipment on the ground, not an orbiting reflector.

Reflect Orbital said the exercise was designed to show how its proposed service could support search-and-rescue operations in remote areas.

“Search-and-rescue teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who would use our technology,” a company spokesperson told The Guardian.

But the demonstration has added to a dispute that began even before the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) authorised the company’s first experimental spacecraft in July this year.

Environmental groups challenge FCC approval

As Aerospace Global News reported in August, the FCC granted Reflect Orbital permission to operate Earendil-1, a satellite designed to deploy an 18-metre by 18-metre reflector and direct sunlight towards selected locations on Earth.

The spacecraft is intended to demonstrate whether reflected sunlight can be controlled accurately enough to support commercial applications, including extending the operating hours of solar farms after sunset.

The FCC authorisation, issued on July 9, covers a single demonstration satellite, not the much larger constellation envisaged by the company.

Four environmental organisations subsequently challenged the decision, arguing that the regulator had failed to consider the potential consequences for astronomy, wildlife and public safety.

DarkSky International, Environment America, the American Bird Conservancy and Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility asked the FCC to reconsider the approval.

Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the groups, delivered a particularly sharp assessment in comments to The Guardian.

“This is an idiotic project,” he said, warning of unresolved questions about its environmental effects.

He argued that the natural cycle of daylight and darkness is fundamental to life on Earth and that large-scale deployment of orbital mirrors could fundamentally alter the night sky.

The environmental groups want the FCC to conduct a broader review before allowing the technology to proceed.

Astronomers warn of damage to observations

Astronomers are particularly concerned about the brightness of the proposed reflectors.

Unlike conventional satellites, which unintentionally reflect sunlight as they pass overhead, Reflect Orbital’s spacecraft would be designed specifically to direct light towards Earth.

Scientists fear that the resulting glare could overwhelm sensitive telescope detectors and compromise observations of faint objects.

Samantha Lawler, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Regina, told NBC News in August that the effects could extend far beyond a satellite’s intended illumination area.

“They have made no indication of how they will coordinate with observatories,” she said. “That could destroy a camera on a telescope. It can also damage people’s eyes.”

Environmental campaigners have raised similar concerns about migratory birds, insects and other nocturnal wildlife that depend on natural darkness for navigation, feeding and reproduction.

There is also the question of who gets to decide where reflected sunlight falls.

A study discussed in an October 26 article by astronomer Richard de Grijs in The Conversation suggests that atmospheric scattering could spread illumination well beyond the intended target. The modelling concerned a proposed larger reflector rather than Earendil-1 itself.

Even communities outside a paying customer’s property could therefore experience additional night-time brightness.

India enters the debate as launch plans advance

On October 14, Reflect Orbital announced that it had purchased two dedicated launches from Indian private space company Skyroot Aerospace to deploy future spacecraft. The first mission will use Skyroot’s Vikram-1 rocket, while the second will fly aboard the more powerful Vikram-1U, which remains under development. The company said the agreement would provide additional launch capacity alongside its planned missions from the United States.

“There’s a real launch capacity shortage right now. We’re excited to work with a new launch provider, Skyroot, to help ensure access to space,” said Reflect Orbital co-founder and CEO Ben Nowack. He added that the company would continue working with astronomers, local communities and regulators as it developed the technology.

Skyroot co-founder and CEO Pawan Kumar Chandana described the agreement as an opportunity to support an ambitious international space project. “We are pleased to partner with Ben and the Reflect Orbital team across two dedicated launches, providing schedule certainty and mission flexibility,” he said.

While the American regulator authorised Earendil-1’s radio communications and satellite operations, the question of who should approve deliberate illumination of the Earth’s surface remains unresolved.

The FCC authorisation specifies an operating altitude of approximately 625 kilometres, but does not constitute a general licence to illuminate locations anywhere in the world.

The proposed Indian launches also raise questions about responsibility when a US-owned satellite, launched from India, directs light towards another country’s territory.

Although a launch has been discussed for the end of 2026, the latest reporting from The Guardian places the initial orbital demonstration in 2027. A firm launch date remains unconfirmed.

Company defends its technology

Reflect Orbital maintains that its technology could help emergency responders, increase renewable electricity generation and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

It has also sought to reassure critics that sensitive locations would be protected.

“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a company spokesperson told The Guardian.

Riyadh airport flight cancellations continue

King Khalid International Airport partially reopened on 25 October, with limited domestic flights and selected international services operated by Saudi carriers. 

Under the airport’s phased reopening plan, Terminal 1 has been designated for domestic services, while Terminal 2 is handling international flights operated by national airlines. 

As we reported yesterday, Yemen’s Houthi movement targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile just a day after the Saudi airport partially resumed operations following weeks of disruption. 

International flight cancellations continue

While King Khalid International Airport has begun a phased reopening, many international airlines are still taking a cautious approach to returning to Riyadh. IndiGo has already extended its suspension of flights to the Saudi capital, and several other carriers continue to review their schedules as they monitor the security situation and operational restrictions.

Airlines also face ongoing regulatory hurdles. Under current NOTAMs, carriers must obtain approval from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) before operating flights to or from Riyadh. The airport also remains unavailable as a diversion option for other flights, limiting flexibility for airline operations.

As a result, the return of international services is expected to be gradual, even as domestic flights and a limited number of international routes continue to restart under the airport’s reopening plan.

Airlines suspending Riyadh flights: Full list of carriers affected Airlines suspending Riyadh flights: Full list of carriers affected

More than 7,800 flights cancelled across Saudi Arabia

The disruption extends well beyond the Saudi capital. According to Cirium, more than 7,800 flights were cancelled across Saudi Arabian airports between 8-25 October. This represented around 45% of all scheduled departures.

Nationwide cancellations peaked on 12 October, when more than 60% of scheduled flights were grounded.

At Dammam’s King Fahd International Airport, 42% of flights were cancelled during the same period, while Nejran Airport recorded a 100% cancellation rate.

The figures highlight the continuing impact on Saudi Arabia’s aviation network, despite efforts to restore operations at Riyadh.

]]> Retiring Indian Air Force chief flies final sortie in the same Kiran trainer he first flew in 1984 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/iaf-chief-ap-singh-final-flight-kiran/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:38:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54437 India’s Air Chief Marshal AP Singh flew his last sortie in uniform aboard the HJT-16 Kiran trainer at the same air force academy where he first took to the skies in January 1984.

The post Retiring Indian Air Force chief flies final sortie in the same Kiran trainer he first flew in 1984 appeared first on AGN.

]]> For Indian Air Force chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, the final flight of his military career was not in a frontline fighter jet, but in the modest training aircraft in which he first learnt to fly more than four decades ago.

On 20 October, Singh returned to the Air Force Academy at Dundigal, near Hyderabad in central India, and climbed aboard an HJT-16 Kiran Mk-1 trainer with the man who had taught him to fly, retired Wing Commander VS Kochar.

The 55-minute sortie brought together the same instructor, the same aircraft type and the same training establishment where Singh had taken his first flying lesson on 28 January 1984.

There was even a familiar aircraft awaiting him. The Kiran used for the flight carried the registration U-707.

Singh, who is due to retire as Chief of the Air Staff on 31 October, had wanted his final sortie in uniform to take him back to where his flying career began.

“It was really a dream come true. I started my journey with the same aircraft,” Singh told reporters after landing, according to news agency ANI.

“I think I must be the only chief who’s retiring while the basic aircraft he flew is still serving.”

For a pilot who has spent more than four decades flying military aircraft, the occasion was as much about the instructor sitting beside him as the aircraft itself.

“I’m very grateful to my instructor, VS Kochar sir, who taught me flying in the beginning in this place itself,” Singh said.

“So I just wanted the circle to be complete. And I did my first sortie on 28 January 1984, in this very place with him, and today I did my last sortie in uniform with him in the same aircraft.”

The instructor who started it all

Flying instructors occupy a special place in military aviation. Long before a pilot learns to operate a fighter aircraft, it is an instructor who introduces them to the fundamentals of flight, teaches them to recognise mistakes and develops the judgement needed to handle an aircraft safely.

For Singh, that instructor was Kochar, who was back in the cockpit with his former pupil after 42 years.

The reunion was equally meaningful for the retired officer.

Kochar, now 73, described Singh as his “brightest pupil ever” and the “best chief”, according to comments reported by the Press Trust of India. He said getting another flight with his former student was a dream come true for him as well.

The two men had returned to the academy in very different circumstances from their first flight together. In 1984, Singh was a young trainee beginning his military flying career. This time, he was returning as the head of the Indian Air Force.

Their flight ended with a ceremonial water cannon salute, with jets of water forming an arch over the aircraft as it returned.

The IAF described the occasion as a tribute to the veterans and flying instructors who have shaped generations of its pilots.

Why the Kiran matters

Developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the Kiran is an Indian-designed, single-engine jet trainer that first flew in 1964. It was introduced to prepare pilots for the transition from basic flying instruction to more demanding military aircraft.

The HJT-16 Kiran has been one of the most recognisable aircraft in Indian military flying training.

Its two-seat cockpit allows an instructor and student to fly together, making it particularly suited to teaching jet handling, instrument flying, aerobatics and formation flying.

Unlike modern combat aircraft, the Kiran was not designed around sophisticated sensors, digital displays or advanced weapons. Its principal purpose was to teach pilots how to fly a jet and develop the skills needed for subsequent operational training.

Over the decades, the aircraft became a familiar sight at Indian Air Force training establishments and served as a stepping stone for generations of fighter pilots.

It was also used by the IAF’s Surya Kiran aerobatic team before the team transitioned to the Hawk advanced jet trainer.

The Kiran’s continued service makes Singh’s final sortie particularly unusual. The aircraft type on which he began flying in 1984 was still available for him to fly in October 2026, more than six decades after the design’s first flight.

The IAF has progressively modernised its training fleet with newer aircraft, including the Pilatus PC-7 Mk II basic trainer and the BAE Systems Hawk advanced jet trainer.

However, the Kiran has remained part of the service’s training history, linking successive generations of pilots.

From trainee pilot to air force chief

Singh graduated from the Air Force Academy in 1984, receiving the Sword of Honour, an award recognising outstanding performance during training.

He was commissioned into the fighter stream of the IAF in December that year.

Over the following decades, he qualified as a flying instructor and experimental test pilot, accumulating several thousand hours of flying experience across fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft.

His career eventually took him to the highest appointment in the service, becoming Chief of the Air Staff in September 2024.

The return to Dundigal came just over a week after another significant flight.

On 12 October, Singh flew his final fighter aircraft sortie in an indigenous Tejas light combat aircraft at Jodhpur Air Force Station during Exercise Tarang Shakti.

That flight marked the conclusion of his time flying frontline fighter aircraft. The Kiran sortie, however, was intended to close his flying career in uniform on a more personal note.

]]> Rafale F5 talks resume as France and UAE revisit fighter partnership https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/france-uae-rafale-f5-talks-resumed/ Mon, 26 Oct 2026 16:02:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54515 Renewed talks on possible UAE involvement in the Rafale F5 programme come months after negotiations stalled over technology-sharing and industrial participation, according to Reuters and French media reports.

The post Rafale F5 talks resume as France and UAE revisit fighter partnership appeared first on AGN.

]]> France and the United Arab Emirates have reopened discussions on possible UAE participation in the Rafale F5 fighter jet programme.

Reuters first reported the revival of the talks on 23 October, citing officials, following French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit to Abu Dhabi.

Reuters reported that France is seeking additional funding sources for the Rafale F5 programme as it pursues several major defence projects simultaneously.

The two countries have a longstanding defence relationship, reinforced by the UAE’s landmark purchase of 80 Rafale fighters in 2021.

According to reports by La Tribune, the earlier talks stalled after disagreements over technology access and industrial participation.

What happened in previous discussions?

Reuters reported that the UAE had been prepared to contribute up to €3.5 billion towards the Rafale F5 programme.

In return, the UAE wanted to participate closely in the aircraft’s development and gain access to technologies arising from the programme.

French financial newspaper La Tribune reported on 2 April that negotiations had become increasingly difficult throughout 2025, culminating in a particularly strained meeting between Macron and UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during the French leader’s visit to Abu Dhabi in December that year.

According to the report, the main disagreement concerned how much technology France was prepared to share.

La Tribune reported that the UAE sought industrial participation and access to technology from the programme, while France was unwilling to grant access to certain sensitive systems, particularly in optronics.

The French side had reportedly considered some cooperation in this area before withdrawing from the proposal.

Abu Dhabi subsequently decided against financing the programme without receiving the technological benefits it had sought.

La Tribune reported that the loss of Emirati funding could force Paris to spread expenditure over a longer period, potentially delaying the introduction of aircraft upgraded to the F5 standard.

A relationship built around 80 Rafale fighters

The UAE is already Dassault Aviation’s largest export customer for the Rafale, having signed a contract for 80 aircraft on 3 December 2021 during Macron’s visit to the country.

The fighter order alone was valued at approximately €14 billion ($15.7 billion). A separate €2 billion ($2.25 billion) agreement covered weapons, while another €1 billion ($1.12 billion) contract provided for 12 Airbus H225M Caracal helicopters. Together, the agreements were worth around €17 billion (around $19 billion).

The UAE had previously considered buying 60 Rafales as early as 2009, but those discussions failed to produce an agreement. The 2021 contract finally secured the aircraft as replacements for the UAE’s ageing Mirage 2000-9 fleet.

The Emirati aircraft are being acquired in the F4 configuration, an upgrade that improves the Rafale’s connectivity, sensors, weapons integration and ability to operate alongside other military assets.

Deliveries were originally scheduled to begin in 2027.

Announcing the 2021 agreement, Dassault Aviation chairman and CEO Eric Trappier described the sale as a continuation of a relationship dating back to earlier French combat aircraft.

“After the Mirage 5 and Mirage 2000, this Rafale contract consolidates the strategic relationship that binds our two countries and the satisfaction of the Emirates Air Force, a long-standing and demanding partner of our company,” he said.

The new F5 discussions concern the development of a more advanced version of the fighter. They do not represent another confirmed aircraft purchase.

What makes the Rafale F5 different?

The Rafale F5 is intended to keep France’s principal combat aircraft effective against increasingly sophisticated air defences and new generations of fighters.

Often referred to as the Super Rafale, the proposed upgrade goes considerably further than improvements to radar, communications and weapons.

It is expected to introduce more advanced sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, artificial intelligence and the ability to operate alongside uncrewed aircraft.

One important objective is to allow a Rafale pilot to work with a combat drone that can carry out reconnaissance or other missions in dangerous airspace.

Such an arrangement could allow the crewed fighter to remain farther from hostile defences while the accompanying drone performs tasks closer to the threat.

France is already pursuing technologies needed for these operations.

As previously reported by AGN, French military officials have outlined plans to use artificial intelligence to improve cooperation between fighters and drones. Dassault has also been involved in testing AI applications aboard the Rafale, while France is working towards a coordinated flight involving a Rafale and an accompanying drone in 2028.

The F5 programme is also expected to support France’s airborne nuclear deterrent through the integration of a future high-speed missile.

Reuters and La Tribune reported that access to sensitive technologies was a central issue in previous negotiations.

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants.                         <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>

                         <p>Incoming mobile students also bring new perspectives to the institution, the local students and the culture which is part of the internationalisation of the receiving institution. This is a significant opportunity to benefit from the experiences that international students bring. To capitalise on these experiences, the institution and its student organisations should put in place opportunities for incoming students to showcase their talent and perspectives through access to existing local initiatives (e.g. school teaching programmes, community projects) and setting up new initiatives to celebrate the different cultures (e.g. theatre performances, food and cultural weeks etc.). Local associations can support the integration of incoming students with the local community, through existing initiatives such as the Social Erasmus and Erasmus in School projects (<a href="http://socialerasmus.esn.org">http://socialerasmus.esn.org</a>).&nbsp;</p><p>Some incoming students may even have been involved in the management or governance of their sending institutions and recognising this opportunity and involving incoming students in similar functions in the receiving institution such as in the student union (elected representative) or working groups dedicated to the voice of the international student.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>                      </div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> At the end of the mobility, your institution has formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to recognition at the end of the mobility, e.g. in the use of Transcripts of Records and Grade Distribution Tables)</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records are issued in a timely manner (normally 5 weeks) to both incoming and outgoing students</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is highly important in the recognition framework to provide Transcripts of Records in a timely manner, immediately following the mobility period. After the mobility, the receiving institution should send a Transcript of Records to the student and to the sending institution within a period stipulated in the Inter-Institutional Agreement (normally within five weeks after publication/proclamation of the student’s results at the receiving institution). It can be provided electronically or through any other means accessible to the student and the sending institution. The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should refer to the educational components agreed upon in the Learning Agreement. Grade distribution information should be included as well, either as a web link or an annex.</p><p>Following the receipt of the Transcript of Records from the receiving institution, the sending institution should automatically transfer and recognise the student’s academic outcomes successfully completed at the receiving institution, as agreed in the Learning Agreement, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The Sending Institution will provide a Transcript of Records to the student or record the results in a database or any other means accessible to the student, normally within five weeks after having received the transcript of the receiving institution. The EU official template for the Learning Agreement for studies (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of incoming students include, where applicable, a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Where applicable, the Sending Institution should translate the grades received by the student abroad. To enable the Sending Institution to do so, it is highly important for the receiving institution to provide a clear explanation of the institutional grading system and grade distribution in the department or study programme together with the Transcript of Records. Such information can be provided either through a web link or as an annex to the Transcripts of Records. Where applicable, use should be made of a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide (<a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm</a>).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All credits gained by students during a period of study abroad that were specified in the final version of the Learning Agreement are automatically transferred by your institution and count towards the students' final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The sending institution should ensure that all the credits earned by the mobile student during the mobility period are recognised and counted towards the final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The period of study abroad must be clear in the student's records and documents issued to the student (Diploma Supplement or equivalent). This is a golden rule of recognition of credit mobility within the framework of inter-institutional agreements. All the credits towards the student's degree that are earned during the mobility period and which were originally agreed on in the Learning Agreement (or a revised version to it) should be recognised by the sending HEI without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. Learning Agreements are binding for all the parties and require that, on successful completion of the mobility period, the sending HEI recognises credits earned by the student and documents these credits in the student records, so they can be identified in a transparent way.</p><p>Upon receipt of the Transcript of Records or Training Certificates, the sending HEI should:<br>a) certify the mobile student has fulfilled all requirements stipulated in the Learning Agreement;<br>b) ensure recognition of the mobility period abroad within the time-scale and according to the conditions stipulated in the institutional recognition framework.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">In addition to recognising formal learning, the institution recognises any non-formal or informal learning acquired during the mobility according to the ECTS Users’ Guide, e.g. by awarding ECTS credits for volunteering</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>During a period of mobility, students often take advantage of other opportunities outside of their required courses. These may include specific activities which can be considered non-formal or informal learning where they have acquired new skills. This could include additional language and cultural courses, extra-curricular activities, setting up a business and volunteer work undertaken by the student in that period or upon return at the receiving institution.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">To all students, automatically, free of charge and in a major European language</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>This Supplement should include a record of the period of mobility under the Erasmus+ Programme. The 48 European countries taking part in the Bologna Process have agreed that each mobile graduate in their respective country should receive the Diploma Supplement (DS) automatically, free of charge and in at least one of the major European languages in addition to the national language. The HEI should issue a Diploma Supplement (or equivalent) to accompany every degree successfully completed by a student, using - where applicable - the template developed by the European Commission, the Council of Europe and UNESCO. The HEI's policy on issuing the Diploma Supplement should be published on its website.</p><p>The template for the Diploma Supplement is available at:<br><a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm&nbsp;</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That includes a record of the mobility period(s) carried out by the student under the Erasmus+ programme</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The information contained in the Transcript of Records from the Receiving Institution should also be included in the Diploma Supplement produced by the Sending Institution (at least for Sending Institutions located in Programme Countries), with the exact titles of the components that the student has followed abroad. Alongside modules or units taken at the sending HEI, the Diploma Supplement should list recognised modules, units and/or training activities undertaken during the student's mobility period and indicate the location of these mobility activities.<br>In the case of double, multiple or joint degrees, the Diploma Supplement should indicate the name and status of the partner HEIs awarding the degree and explain the respective language(s) of instruction and examination. In addition, an explanation should be provided about the grading and classification scheme agreed by the awarding HEIs. The template for the Diploma Supplement is available at:<br><a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/tools/diploma-supplement_en.htm</a>&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

            </div>
